title: Generic and specific gravity of the offending
statement: Generic gravity is reflected in the maximum penalty and the elements of the offence. The court must also assess the gravity of the specific offending relative to other examples of the offence, by identifying its particulars (e.g. planning, method, abuse of trust), its explanation (mitigatory factors that reduce moral culpability but not offence gravity) and its consequences (for the victim, the community or society).

refs.q: The generic gravity of an offence is reflected in the maximum penalty fixed by Parliament and in the elements of the crime
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

refs.q: However, a court must also assess the gravity of the specific offending falling for sentence. That requires it to assess the relative gravity of the offending with other examples of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

refs.q: The first step in doing that is to identify the relevant circumstances of the offending which includes its particulars (such as planning, method, abuse of trust etc.), its explanation (such as the existence of mitigatory factors that reduce moral culpability but not offence gravity), and its consequences (be it on the victim, the community or society).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

refs.q: In identifying the relevant circumstances, a court has broad latitude subject to a few firm limits.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

title: The maximum penalty: absolute limit, Parliament’s view, mandatory consideration
statement: Unless an indefinite sentence is available, the maximum is the absolute highest term, indicates Parliament’s view of the gravity of the offence and is a mandatory consideration. It is a navigational aid (the court steers by it, not towards it) that always requires careful attention. The court must place the offence and offender on a spectrum from the least serious instance of the offence to the worst.

refs.q: Unless an indefinite sentence is available under the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) s 18A (‘the Act’) the maximum penalty fixed by Parliament is: • absolutely the highest term that may be imposed for the offence; • indicates Parliament’s view of the gravity of the offence; and • a mandatory consideration for a court in determining the appropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty

refs.q: It reflects Parliament’s view of the gravity of the offending but is also ‘an aspect of the duty of all courts not to exceed their jurisdiction or powers’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: The maximum penalty set by Parliament is a lighthouse, and like a ship, the court does not steer towards it but by it. It is a navigational aid, not an end in itself,
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: but careful attention to the maximum is always required.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: A court must assess where the circumstances of the offence and the offender fall along a spectrum of least serious instance of the offence to worst.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

title: Where maximum penalties are found
statement: Maximum penalties are found at the foot of the section for statutory indictable offences and in the offence-specific chapters of the Manual (offences.json in this knowledge base). In Victoria the maximum is often expressed as a “level” or “unit” (the penalty scale), but some legislation still states it in years or months (where the two are inconsistent the level prevails unless there is a contrary intention: audit.level_term_mismatch).

refs.q: • at the foot of the individual section for statutory indictable offences; and • in the offence specific chapters of this Manual.

refs.q: This will rarely arise as penalties for most common law offences have now been defined by statute.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.1 – Identifying the maximum penalty

title: “Worst category” is reserved for cases warranting the maximum
statement: Offending that does not warrant the maximum should not be described as “within the worst category”; the phrase is reserved for cases where the maximum is warranted and should not be used as shorthand. It is better to say whether the offending is so grave as to warrant the maximum or not.

refs.q: Despite practices in the past, offences that do not warrant the maximum penalty should not be referred to as being ‘within the worst category’. That description should be reserved for cases where the maximum penalty is warranted.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: A court should also avoid using ‘within the worst category’ as a ‘convenient form of legal shorthand’ because it may lead the public to believe the court has undervalued the gravity of the offending and its effects.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: It is better for a court to simply state, when relevant, whether the offending is so grave as to warrant the maximum penalty or not.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

title: Factors relevant to whether the maximum penalty is called for
statement: Factors relevant to whether the maximum is called for include role, drug quantity/value/sophistication/international scope, relevant prior history, the stage of any plea, genuine remorse, commercial motive, delay, and (for child sexual offending and for rape and other sexual offences) the specific features listed.

refs.q: the offender’s role (principal or subordinate) in the offending;

refs.q: for drug offences: the quantity and value of the drugs, the sophistication of the operation, and its international scope;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: for sexual offending against children, including incest: the existence or lack of grooming, predatory behaviour, if the offender was in a position of authority that was exploited, the vulnerability of the victim, the age of the child, the existence and explicitness of any images, whether there was penetration, was the child isolated or manipulated, was the offending consistent, the duration of the offending, the depravity and degradation of the acts, the location of the offending, and the offender’s disregard for the impact of their actions on the child;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: for rape and other sexual offences: whether the offender was known to the victim, if the victim was overpowered, the location of the attack, the duration of the offending, the violence of the offending, the impact upon the victim, if the offending was committed in company, if the offence was planned, whether the offender was a serious offender, if the offending was predatory or persistent, whether there was penetration and if so by what means, if the offending consisted of multiple attacks, whether the victim suffered any injuries, and whether a weapon was used.

refs.q: Factors relevant to determining if the maximum penalty is called for include:

title: Indictable offence that could have been tried summarily
statement: If an indictable offence might have been tried summarily but was not, the court may consider that fact, but it is not limited to the maximum available in the summary jurisdiction.

refs.q: If an indictable offence might be tried summarily, but is not, it is appropriate for a court to consider this fact, but it does not mean it is limited to the maximum sentence that could be imposed in the summary jurisdiction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

use: Python takes the maximum from offences.json for the offence date; auditor confirms the reasoning used it
title: Misidentifying the maximum is appealable error unless immaterial
statement: Misidentifying the applicable maximum is an appealable error unless shown to be immaterial. Indicators of material effect: the sentence is a high percentage of the wrongly believed maximum; the affected charges are a large part of the total effective sentence; the court appeared influenced by the wrong maximum; or the error cannot be disregarded (e.g. imprisonment imposed where the maximum is a fine).

refs.q: Misidentifying the applicable maximum penalty is an appealable error unless it can be shown to be immaterial.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: • the sentence imposed represents a high percentage of what the court erroneously believed the maximum to be; • the sentences imposed for charges where the maximum was incorrect represented a large part of the total effective sentence; • the court appeared to have been influenced by the incorrect maximum;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: the error cannot be disregarded, such as when the sentence imposed is imprisonment, but the maximum is a fine.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: Indicators that there has been a material effect on the sentence include where:

use: offence-date logic when selecting the maximum from offences.json
title: Changes to the maximum penalty between offence and sentence
statement: For offences before a change: apply any reduction, never an increase. If the maximum was reduced then increased between offence and sentence, the court need not apply the temporarily reduced maximum and may use the original if the current penalty is of the same magnitude or higher. For offences after a change: the change reflects Parliament’s new assessment; an increase signals existing sentences were insufficient and should increase. A repealed offence keeps its maximum for conduct under it; a new similar offence does not affect it.
logic: ceiling = min(max_at_offence_date, every maximum in force between the offence date and sentence) — any reduction applies, no increase does; exception (one implementation shared with audit.maximum_applicable step (2)): if the maximum was reduced and later increased before sentence AND current_max >= max_at_offence_date, the court may sentence up to max_at_offence_date (a sentence within the reduced maximum also passes); if the later increase stops below the original, the general rule governs (ceiling = the reduced maximum)

refs.q: For offences occurring before the date of a change of penalty, the court must sentence in accordance with any reduction in maximum penalty but must not consider any increase in maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.3 – Effects of alterations to maximum penalty

refs.q: One exception to this rule is where the maximum penalty is reduced then increased between the date of offending and the date of sentence. In that situation, the court is not required to take into account the temporarily reduced penalty and may instead sentence in accordance with the original maximum penalty, if the current penalty is of the same magnitude or higher.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.3 – Effects of alterations to maximum penalty

refs.q: For offences occurring after a change to the maximum penalty, the court must take into account that change as reflecting Parliament’s new assessment of the seriousness of the offence. Where the penalty is increased, courts must treat that as a signal by Parliament that existing sentences have been insufficient and should be increased.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.3 – Effects of alterations to maximum penalty

refs.q: If an offence has been repealed, the maximum penalty for that repealed offence continues to apply to conduct under the old offence. The enactment of a new offence for similar conduct has no impact on the assessment of maximum penalty for the old offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.3 – Effects of alterations to maximum penalty

title: Statutory factors bearing on gravity (s 5(2))
statement: The Act lists non-exclusive circumstances: nature and gravity; culpability and degree of responsibility; hatred or prejudice motive; impact on the victim; circumstances of the victim; injury, loss or damage resulting directly; aggravating or mitigating circumstances; any other relevant circumstances. Generally, gravity is informed by the degree of risk of harm and the extent of potential harm, assessed on the individual circumstances; the factors overlap with the offender’s circumstances and the purposes and principles.

refs.q: The Act prescribes a number of non-exclusive circumstances relevant to determining the gravity of offending, including: • its nature and gravity; • the offender’s culpability and degree of responsibility for the offence; • whether the offending was motivated, wholly or partly, by hatred or prejudice against a group of people with whom the victim was associated or the offender believed they were associated; • its impact on the victim; • the circumstances of the victim; • any injury, loss, or damage resulting directly from the offending; • any aggravating or mitigating circumstances of the offender; • ‘or of any other relevant circumstances’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors

refs.q: Generally, a court’s assessment of gravity ‘is informed by the degree of risk of harm being caused and the extent of the potential harm’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors

refs.q: The seriousness of an offence should be assessed on the individual circumstances of the case, even if multiple categories of offending might be covered by one offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors

refs.q: It is also important to remember in considering the gravity of the offending that there will frequently be overlap with the circumstances of the offender, the sentencing purposes and principles, and that lines between each may not be easily drawn.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors

title: Planning, duration, scale and sophistication
statement: Premeditated or planned offending (even if inept or unsuccessful) is usually more serious than spontaneous, opportunistic or unplanned offending; generally the greater the planning, duration, scale and sophistication, the graver the offending, and it also invokes general deterrence and community protection. But the Court of Appeal has also said there may often be little to distinguish a premeditated attack from a random one of sustained violence; the Manual suggests (“it seems”) the Court was reinforcing the need to condemn public and family violence regardless of planning. In quantity-based offending (drug trafficking/importation) quantity is more significant than duration or number of transactions and is a key indicator of gravity.

refs.q: A premeditated or planned offence (even if inept or unsuccessful) is usually considered to be more serious than one that is spontaneous, opportunistic or unplanned, even if violent.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.1 – Planning and scale

refs.q: However, while it may seem contradictory, the Court of Appeal has also said there may often be little to distinguish between the culpability of a premeditated attack and a random one of sustained violence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.1 – Planning and scale

refs.q: In doing so it seems the Court was reinforcing the need to strongly condemn the gravity of violence occurring either in public or in the family context regardless of a lack of planning by the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.1 – Planning and scale

refs.q: But, generally, the greater the planning, duration, and scale of the offending, and the more sophisticated its method, the more gravely it will be considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.1 – Planning and scale

refs.q: This is particularly so for quantity-based offending, such as drug trafficking or importation, where the quantity trafficked (or manufactured, as actual distribution is not required) or imported is more significant than other factors, such as duration or number of transactions, and is a key indicator of the gravity of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.1 – Planning and scale

refs.q: It also invokes the need for general deterrence and community protection.

title: Intent, recklessness and knowledge of risk
statement: All things being equal, intentional offending attracts a higher sentence than reckless offending. Acting with knowledge of a possible risk increases culpability, particularly knowledge of a large-scale risk or separate attacks of escalating violence. Impaired decision-making may reduce the level of recklessness depending on the impairment. Knowledge of risk must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

refs.q: All things being equal, intentional offending should attract a higher sentence than reckless offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

refs.q: Similarly, someone who acts with knowledge of a possible risk has greater culpability than someone who does not, and particularly if their knowledge is of a ‘large-scale risk’ as opposed to a ‘small risk’ or involves separate attacks of escalating violence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

refs.q: The level of recklessness may be reduced if the offender’s decision making is impaired, but this will depend on the nature and severity of the impairment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

refs.q: The offender’s knowledge of risk or its possibility must be established by evidence beyond a reasonable doubt.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

title: Repetitive or persistent (versus intermittent) offending
statement: Repetitive or persistent offending increases culpability (knowledge of unlawfulness, failure to take the opportunity to cease, fear engendered in victims and community); intermittent offending is less serious.

refs.q: Repetitive or persistent offending increases culpability because of the offender’s knowledge of its unlawfulness and their failure to take the opportunity to cease, as well as the fear it engenders in victims and the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

refs.q: By contrast intermittent offending is less serious.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.2 – Intent and knowledge

title: Role in offending with co-offenders
statement: Each participant’s role must generally be assessed: a subordinate or non-consequential role generally reduces culpability; a substantial or leading role may increase it. For offences of great magnitude (terrorism, drug trafficking) any involvement indicates high moral culpability. Never lose sight of the offence charged and what the offender actually did. Do not place excessive weight on positioning the offender in a notional hierarchy (e.g. drug roles). Without evidence the court need not make a favourable finding; distinctions between co-offenders (important for parity) need an evidentiary basis.

cautions.text: Do not place excessive weight on hierarchies of roles.

refs.q: One circumstance where a court will often be asked to make findings about an offender’s role is where different identified roles have been placed in a notional hierarchy of culpability.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: Drug offending is the prime example of this approach, but the High Court has warned against placing excessive weight on the task of positioning offenders within these hierarchies.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

cautions.text: No favourable finding is required in the absence of evidence.

refs.q: If those circumstances are not established by material before the court, it is not required to inquire into the facts and in the absence of evidence is not required to make a finding favourable to the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

cautions.text: Distinctions between co-offenders need an evidentiary basis.

refs.q: Such distinctions can be particularly important when parity is an issue, but there must be an evidentiary basis for establishing such differences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: For offending committed by multiple co-offenders, it is generally necessary to assess each participant’s role. Depending on the circumstances, this consideration may magnify or reduce their culpability. Where an offender takes a subordinate or non-consequential role, their culpability for the offence will generally be reduced. Where the offender’s role is substantial or leading, their culpability may be increased.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: The magnitude of certain offences, such as terrorism or drug trafficking, is such that any involvement in it indicates a high degree of moral culpability and calls for a heavy penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: However, in seeking to identify the offender’s role, a court should never lose sight of the particular offence charged, and what the particular offender actually did.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

title: Principal and accessory but unknown which is which
statement: Where the evidence shows one joint offender was a principal and another an accessory but not which was which, both are treated as no more culpable than an accessory. This does not apply where there is no evidence of a distinction, and an accessory’s culpability is not presumptively lower than a principal’s.

refs.q: Where evidence establishes that one joint offender was a principal, and another an accessory, but it cannot be determined which offender was which, then both must be treated as being no more culpable than an accessory.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: This does not apply when there is no evidence of a distinction between the two offenders, nor should it be assumed that an accessory’s culpability is presumptively lower than a principal’s culpability.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

title: Abuse of status or position; breach of trust
statement: Abuse or misuse of status or position, particularly a breach of trust, may aggravate objective seriousness — e.g. offending by those in the justice system, public officials, a parent or carer against a child, a family friend sexually offending against a child, and persons in positions of trust (teachers, doctors, employees, others).

refs.q: offending by individuals within the justice system, such as police officers, judges, lawyers;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: offending by public officials and public servants;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

examples.text: parent/carer against a child (incest, other sexual offending, manslaughter)

refs.q: offending by a parent, or other person with the care, supervision or custody of, against a child, as in cases of incest or other sexual offending and manslaughter;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: sexual offending against a child by a family friend;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

examples.text: positions of trust (teachers, doctors, employees, others)

refs.q: offending by persons in positions of trust, such as teachers, doctors, and employees, and others.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

cautions.text: Breach of trust cannot be used both as an aggravating factor and to diminish good character (see factor.good_character).

refs.q: But undue weight cannot be given to an offender’s breach of trust. It cannot be used both as an aggravating factor and to diminish an offender’s good character.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

cautions.text: A justice-system or government status may also be an offender aggravator under factor.employment (6.3.3.2); count one status or abuse-of-position fact once (audit.double_punishment).

refs.q: Clearly, it is also subjectively relevant to the offender.

There are also professions associated with government and the justice system whose members are expected to act with highest levels of honesty and integrity, and their failure to do so may be taken as an aggravating factor and emphasise the need for just punishment and general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.2 – Employment

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

title: Provocation
statement: Provocation by the victim may lessen culpability but not the significance of the harm. Its weight is a matter of degree and circumstance: a sudden or spontaneous loss of control (particularly from fear rather than anger) may reduce culpability; mitigation is limited where the response reflects an inability to control anger or is wholly disproportionate; time elapsed does not of itself remove it. In a family relationship, provocation or emotional stress is subordinate to general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment unless the offending stems from fear rather than anger.

refs.q: If the victim provokes offending conduct, it may lessen an offender’s culpability, but it does not lessen the significance of any harm suffered by the victim.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.4 – Provocation

refs.q: With the abolition of provocation as a defence to murder, provocation considerations are now confined to sentencing. The weight to be given to this issue is a matter of degree and circumstance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.4 – Provocation

refs.q: if the offence is committed under provocation, it mitigates the seriousness of the offence and may reduce the offender’s culpability,
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.4 – Provocation

refs.q: on offender may be seen as less morally culpable if they suffered a sudden or spontaneous loss of control in response to provocation, particularly if their conduct was the product of fear rather than anger,

title: Hatred or prejudice motive (s 5(2)(daaa))
statement: If the offending was wholly or partly motivated by hatred for or prejudice against a group of people with common characteristics, that aggravates gravity and moral culpability. Groups are not limited by the Act (the second reading speech identified religious affiliation, racial or cultural origin, sexual orientation, sex, gender identity, age, impairment and homelessness) and are determined case by case. The victim may be a member of the group, a “Good Samaritan”, an advocate, someone employed in relation to the group, or an acquaintance or family member. There has been little judicial consideration of the provision: one case held the motive must be proved beyond reasonable doubt (consistent with findings.formosa); in another, intoxication and a drug-induced psychosis did not obviate the stated motivation, though such matters may reduce its aggravating force.

refs.q: Section 5(2)(daaa) of the Act requires a sentencing court to consider if ‘hatred for or prejudice against a group of people with common characteristics’ motivated (or partly motivated) the offending. If so, then it is as an aggravating factor, which increases the gravity of the offence and the moral culpability of the offender.

title: Circumstances of the victim (general)
statement: The victim’s circumstances are highly significant to gravity; harm is usually the most important, with vulnerability, protected class, conduct, relationship to the offender and sometimes attitude to sentence. Where harm is an element of the offence, Parliament has already taken it into account in the maximum, so it must not be doubly weighed. “Victim” is construed broadly (direct victim, family, secondary victims such as witnesses, society or the community; there may be several victims).

refs.q: The circumstances of the victim are highly significant in determining the gravity of any offence, with the most important consideration usually being any harm to them. Other considerations include the victim’s vulnerability, whether they are in a protected class, their conduct, relationship to the offender, and, in some instances, their attitude to the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.6 – Impact on and circumstances of the victim

refs.q: But, as discussed further below, a statute may specify that harm to the victim is an element of an offence and if it does, then Parliament has already taken their harm into account in fixing a maximum penalty and a court must then be careful not to doubly weigh harm in determining the appropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.6 – Impact on and circumstances of the victim

refs.q: ‘Victim’ is construed broadly to include the direct victim, their family, or secondary victims like witnesses; a victim can also be society or the community, and there can be more than one victim in either a single offence or multiple offences.

Where a victim characteristic (e.g. a child’s age) is an element of the offence charged, it cannot also be counted as aggravating, although conduct that exceeds the minimum needed to satisfy an element can indicate a more serious example of the offence (factor.element_not_aggravating).

title: Protected persons as victims

title: Relationship between offender and victim (domestic context; innocent stranger)
note: The direction tag captures the firm rule (a domestic context is never mitigating); the statement governs: a domestic context may also aggravate, and offending against an innocent stranger is treated as serious.
statement: A relationship may be relevant to gravity. Offending in a domestic context can never be mitigating and may be aggravating, particularly family violence, rape or other sexual offending. The absence of any relationship may also be significant: offending against an “innocent stranger” is serious.

refs.q: The existence of a relationship between the offender and the victim may be relevant in assessing the gravity of the offending. Offending in a domestic context can never be mitigating and may be aggravating, particularly in cases of family violence, rape, or other sexual offending.

title: Victim’s conduct
statement: A victim’s conduct, if established on the balance of probabilities, may bear on sentence even if it does not lessen moral culpability or gravity. It is unhelpful to label it mitigating or otherwise, or to call the victim “complicit”. Weight is a matter for the court in the circumstances.

refs.q: A victim’s conduct, if established by a balance of probabilities, may have bearing on the sentence, even if it does not lessen the offender’s moral culpability or affect the gravity of the offending.

title: Victim’s attitude to sentence; forgiveness; no victim impact statement
statement: Generally a victim’s attitude to sentence is irrelevant, but forgiveness may indicate the effects were not long lasting and suffering is lessened; it is of greater relevance for negligence offences. Treat forgiveness cautiously, and with extreme caution in family violence. A victim’s failure to make a victim impact statement or take part is not mitigating.

title: Harm: injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offence
statement: The nature and degree of harm is highly relevant to gravity (physical/psychological; transient to permanent; for endangerment offences the risk created; for dishonesty offences financial loss). The Act requires consideration of impact on the victim and injury, loss or damage resulting directly, whether or not reasonably foreseeable or intended. The prosecution must show a temporal or other connection establishing the harm was the direct result of the offending. Evidence of harm is normally led at trial or, on a plea, in the depositions; where the court must look beyond these, most often through victim impact statements; absent those, the court may draw reasonable inferences (particularly in sexual offending).

cautions.text: Where harm is an element of the offence, do not doubly weigh it.

title: Use of a weapon
statement: Use of a weapon is relevant to gravity: the more dangerous the item and the greater its capacity to invoke fear, the more serious. The use made of it matters — more serious when used to overcome resistance, obtain submission in sexual offences, instil fear and enforce demands, attack or harm the victim, in a public place or at a busy time, or against vulnerable victims or those protected by law. Little or no distinction is generally drawn between imitation and real weapons, though some authority treats an imitation or unloaded weapon as less serious.

title: Benefit to the offender and loss to the victim
statement: Benefit gained and loss caused help assess gravity (property offences; offending for reward such as trafficking). Make reasonable efforts to value property, though quantum errors may be immaterial and value is one guide only. Broad regard may be had to profit if reliable information is available, without detailed examination of illegal dealings; co-offenders may be assumed to share equally absent contrary evidence. Actual enrichment may significantly aggravate; benefit includes benefit to dependants; lack of actual enrichment (e.g. failed offending) is not necessarily mitigating. Lower-level participants who benefit less are less culpable. Failure to quantify loss may limit the available range. Recoupment by insurer or indemnity fund carries little or no mitigating weight if it merely shifts the loss (compare 6.3.4.2 on restitution by third parties: flag.third_party_restitution_weight).

refs.q: The gravity of many offences can be assessed by any benefit gained by an offender and any loss suffered by the victim.

title: Family violence
statement: Victorian courts repeatedly emphasise the need to strongly condemn family violence (breach of trust, gravity of harm, vulnerability of victims); denunciation, just punishment and general deterrence have primacy. Gravity increases if the offending breaches a family violence intervention order or is committed in front of children. Family violence includes physically, sexually, emotionally, psychologically and economically abusive, threatening or coercive behaviour; the surrounding behaviours must be considered to assess true gravity, which is not measured solely by physical consequences, and individual charges are not divorced from the context of control and fear. The community abhors such conduct. Related rules: provocation or emotional stress in a family relationship is subordinate to general deterrence, denunciation and just punishment unless the offending stems from fear rather than anger (factor.provocation); forgiveness is treated with extreme caution; childhood disadvantage cannot reduce the protection due to victims of domestic violence; where the charge is itself a breach of a family violence intervention order, that breach is an element (factor.element_not_aggravating).

refs.q: For numerous reasons – including the breaches of trust involved, the gravity of the harm caused, and the vulnerability of its victims – Victorian courts have repeatedly emphasised the need to strongly condemn family violence.

refs.q: Family violence ‘undermines the foundations of personal relationships and family trust upon which our society rests…,’ and so requires that denunciation, just punishment and general deterrence be given primacy in sentencing in this context.

refs.q: For these same reasons, the gravity of the offending will be increased if the offending breaches a family violence intervention order or is committed in front of children.

refs.q: So it follows that in assessing the totality of the circumstances for an offence committed in the context of family violence, ‘the surrounding behaviours of the offender must be considered to assess the true gravity of the offending’.

The gravity of family violence is not to be measured solely by the physical consequences. The offending as a whole cannot be deconstructed in order to divorce individual charges from a context of degradation, control, threats, and creating an environment of fear and dread.

title: Entrapment by police
statement: Entrapment is not a defence but police entrapping conduct may mitigate. A real possibility that the offending would not have occurred but for police involvement may carry some weight; the focus is its bearing on culpability (from very little to substantial). Relevant: how police contributed, any coercion/pressure/inducement and its degree, whether direct or through an intermediary (more remote, less weight); little weight if the offender instigated, more if their will was overborne.

refs.q: Entrapment is not a defence but entrapping conduct by police may be relevant to mitigation.

title: Uncharged conduct and surrounding facts (no punishment for a more serious uncharged offence)
statement: Uncharged or discreditable conduct may aggravate and indicate increased culpability, but not where it constitutes an aggravated version of the offence, should have been a separate charge, or would warrant conviction for a more serious offence. Considering a victim’s injury when sentencing for recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk, where no separate charge was brought for the injury, does not infringe that principle; but conduct separately sentenced cannot also be used (double punishment). The Manual notes contrary authority for the conditional-liberty and enlisting-others-to-lie examples (fns 1006, 1007). The line is a matter of degree (“fine line”), depending on contemporaneity and the disparity in seriousness. Permissible examples: concealment (disposing of a body, denying knowledge of whereabouts); delaying or preventing medical assistance; lying or enlisting others to lie; offending while on conditional liberty or in contravention of court orders. Highly fact-dependent; the court may decline a negative inference where there is another explanation.

title: Current sentencing practices: mandatory but only one factor
statement: The court must have regard to current sentencing practices (“the approach currently adopted by sentencing judges when sentencing for the particular offence”), but it is one factor among many. The aim is consistency in applying legal principle (like cases alike, different cases differently) — consistency is described as an aspect of the rule of law (the footnote for that statement is unreliable: flag.fn1012_ibid_pinpoint). A range contrary to principle (e.g. insufficient regard to the maximum or the seriousness of the offence) should not be followed, and a court should not consider cases having idiosyncratic features (they are unlikely to be useful comparators).

refs.q: A court must also have regard to current sentencing practices.

title: After Dalgliesh: practices are one consideration; appellate calls for change apply immediately
statement: Before Dalgliesh (HCA), current sentencing practices were treated as a primary consideration and the Court of Appeal would on occasion declare practices for an offence inadequate — where the maximum had been increased and practices did not reflect it; the offence had become more prevalent; community attitudes to its gravity had changed or concern had been expressed; its impact on victims was better understood; a category of offenders had persistently been given too much weight for mitigation (e.g. good character in white-collar crime or culpable driving); or the seriousness of conduct had been wrongly categorised or a disposition was not ordinarily appropriate. Such statements were applied incrementally. That approach is no longer followed: practices are merely one consideration and, where an appellate court indicates practices must change, sentencing courts give effect to it immediately.

refs.q: Before Dalgliesh HCA, courts in Victoria treated current sentencing practices as a primary consideration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: Previously, Court of Appeal statements that sentencing practices for offences were inadequate were meant to be applied incrementally, or progressively, following the appellate decision holding them to be so.

refs.q: Dalgliesh HCA and subsequent Court of Appeal decisions have made it plain this approach is no longer to be followed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: Now, current sentencing practices are merely one consideration among many and, where an appellate court has indicated that sentencing practices need to change, sentencing courts should immediately give effect to that decision.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: The Court would do this where: • the maximum penalty for an offence was increased and sentencing practices did not reflect the increase; • there was evidence that an offence had become more prevalent; • community attitudes regarding the relative gravity of a specific offence changed, thereby impacting on the length of sentence considered appropriate; • the community expressed concerns regarding a particular offence; • the impact of the offence on the victim was better understood; • a category of offenders had been persistently treated erroneously, with too much weight being given to mitigating factors (for example, too much weight being ascribed to good character in the case of those sentenced for white collar crimes or culpable driving); or • the objective seriousness of particular conduct had been wrongly categorised, or a particular type of sentencing disposition was not ordinarily appropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: To address the need for sentencing practices to remain current and respond to changing conditions, the Court of Appeal would, on occasion, express the view that sentencing practices for an offence, or class of offences, were inadequate and needed to increase.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: The purpose was to allow sentencing practice to gradually approach a range that better accorded with the gravity of offending, while not being unduly unfair to an offender who expected to be sentenced according to the range established by past cases.

title: Historic offences: current practices at sentencing, with the maximum at the time of offending
statement: “Current sentencing practices” are those at the time of sentencing (including the weight given to particular considerations), used alongside awareness of the maximum at the time of offending — with caution where the maximum is now higher. Equal justice may require regard to historical practices so far as they can be established and show a materially lesser sanction, if reasonably practicable; it is not an inflexible rule.

refs.q: When sentencing for historic offences the Court of Appeal has concluded that for the purposes of the Act, ‘current sentencing practices’ refers to those in effect at the time of sentencing, not those which existed at the time an offence was committed.

use: governs how the app presents cosine-similar case summaries
title: Comparable cases: “relevantly comparable or instructively different”
statement: Case comparisons are an important primary resource but help only if relevantly comparable or instructively different. Comparability depends on the circumstances of the offender and the offending (generally the same category of seriousness), not merely the same physical conduct. A party relying on cases must identify them and spell out what makes them comparable; a bare list or table of sentences is not enough — tables must explain each case’s key features; references are useful only if they articulate unifying principles. They are a yardstick. Where a party relies on a strikingly similar case, the judge must ordinarily explain how it informed the discretion.

refs.q: Case comparisons are an important primary resource for determining current sentencing practices. However, they will only be helpful when the cases being considered are ‘relevantly comparable or instructively different’.

refs.q: Comparable cases generally involve offending in the same category of seriousness. It is the circumstances of the offender and the offending that determine whether they are ‘relevantly comparable’. The mere fact that the same physical conduct exists in two cases does not mean they are ‘relevantly comparable’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has said that to the extent counsel is relying on comparable cases they must identify the cases and ‘spell out’ what makes them so. Simply providing a list or table of past sentences for a given offence is not enough. Tables of recorded cases will only be useful if they provide more information than just the sentence imposed. They must also explain the key features of each case, to assist a court in understanding the extent to which the case is (or is not) comparable.

refs.q: References to other cases are only useful if they articulate the unifying principles that the disparate sentences reveal.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

title: Comparables should be for the same offence (rare exceptions)
statement: Have strict regard to the offence under consideration; only rarely consider sentences for a different offence, most commonly for quantity-based drug schemes.

refs.q: The Court has also stated that when considering comparable cases, it is important to have strict regard to the offence under consideration. However, in rare instances it will be appropriate for a court to consider sentences imposed for a different offence to the one currently being sentenced, as part of its consideration of current sentencing practice. This is most common for quantity-based offences, such as drug offence schemes that increase in severity depending on the amount of drug imported.

use: auditor: flags reasoning that treats retrieved cases as a binding range or derives a range from a few cases
title: Limitations of case comparisons
statement: Use comparisons cautiously: a past range does not set the outer limits of the discretion or confirm the range is correct; a range should not be defined by a few cases (at most they are points on a spectrum); truly comparable cases are hard to find, especially for extremely serious offending with limited mitigation; do not analyse similar cases in detail to find the “right” sentence or a confined range — they are not binding precedent. Comparisons are of particularly limited use where circumstances vary greatly (manslaughter, intentionally causing serious injury, assault with intent to commit a sexual offence). Great caution with cases predating an appellate declaration of inadequacy. Victorian courts rarely look to other States’ practices.

refs.q: Courts should use case comparisons cautiously. While past comparable cases may indicate a range of sentences that have been imposed in similar matters, that range does not set the outer limits for exercising the sentencing discretion. It also does not confirm that a range or its boundaries are correct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Similarly, the sentencing range should not be defined by only a few select cases. It will not be possible to discern a ‘sentencing practice’ for an offence when there are only a small number of sentences that have been imposed. At most, where only a few cases are relevantly comparable, they may represent points along a spectrum of seriousness, and it may be misleading to give too much weight to comparisons between them.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: As each case is unique, it can be difficult to find truly comparable cases where the gravity of the offending and the circumstances of the offender are similar. This is particularly relevant when the offending is extremely serious, and the offender’s has limited mitigating circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Moreover, a court should not engage in a detailed analysis of similar cases to conclude that a specific sentence is the ‘right one’ or that a sentence should fall within a confined range. Doing so ignores the fact that sentences imposed in other cases are not binding precedent.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Case comparisons are of particularly limited use when the nature of an offence means that the circumstances in which it is committed vary greatly, for example, cases of manslaughter, intentionally causing serious injury, and assault with intent to commit a sexual offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Great caution is required with cases that predate an appellate decision that declared that current sentencing practices for the offence in question were inadequate. However, cases that demonstrate past practices might be relevant to show that the present sentence has not paid sufficient regard for the need to increase current practices.

use: auditor: flags median-anchoring or reliance on statistics alone
title: Sentencing statistics and medians
statement: Statistics are a primary resource and, used correctly, a valuable yardstick, but alone they cannot establish a practice. Shortcomings: they do not identify the appropriate range; may distract from the circumstances; cannot substitute for the instinctive synthesis; alone cannot show manifest excess; cannot analyse wide-ranging offences; say nothing about why sentences were fixed. A median is an accidental or contingent statistic, not a measure of seriousness, and cannot represent the sentence for mid-range offending; selecting a median and asking whether the offending is above or below it risks an improper two-stage approach. Permitted uses: courts have used statistics to help check whether a sentence accords with current practices, and appellate courts to check whether a consideration (e.g. youth) was given too little or too much weight.

refs.q: Another primary resource for determining sentencing practices are sentencing statistics. Statistics alone, however, are insufficient to establish sentencing practices and there are important limitations to their use. Nonetheless, if used correctly, sentencing statistics can also act as a ‘valuable yardstick’, against which to measure a particular sentence.

title: Generic gravity (maximum and elements) and specific gravity
statement: In considering the circumstances of the offence the court largely considers gravity from a generic and a specific perspective, which cannot be neatly divided. Generic gravity is reflected in the maximum penalty and the elements of the offence. The maximum is a mandatory consideration; the effect of a change in the maximum depends on the nature of the change and the date of offending.

refs.q: When a court considers the circumstances of the offence it is largely considering the gravity of the offending from both a generic and specific perspective, even though the two cannot be neatly divided.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

refs.q: The generic gravity of an offence is reflected in the maximum penalty fixed by Parliament and in the elements of the crime and it is on these factors that a court will typically rely in making an initial pronouncement, such as ‘murder is a most serious offence’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence

refs.q: Firstly, as noted, the maximum penalty is a mandatory consideration under the Act for a court determining an appropriate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.2 – Significance of maximum penalty

refs.q: The impact of changes to the maximum penalty for an offence vary depending on the nature of the change and the date of offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.1 – Maximum penalty > 5.1.3 – Effects of alterations to maximum penalty

title: Distinguishing co-offenders’ roles needs an evidentiary basis
statement: Excessive weight should not be placed on positioning offenders in hierarchies of culpability, since a role may be known only after examining all the circumstances; absent evidence the court need not make a favourable finding. Distinctions between offenders by role in the same enterprise can still be drawn, and matter especially for parity, but must have an evidentiary basis.

refs.q: If those circumstances are not established by material before the court, it is not required to inquire into the facts and in the absence of evidence is not required to make a finding favourable to the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: This does not mean distinctions cannot be drawn between multiple offenders based on their roles in the same enterprise. Such distinctions can be particularly important when parity is an issue, but there must be an evidentiary basis for establishing such differences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: Drug offending is the prime example of this approach, but the High Court has warned against placing excessive weight on the task of positioning offenders within these hierarchies.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

refs.q: This is because an offender’s role might only be fully known after examining all of the circumstances, including those surrounding, but not necessarily constituting part of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.3 – Role and status

title: Hatred or prejudice motive: groups not limited; intoxication or psychosis does not negate a stated motive
statement: The Act does not identify or limit the groups sharing “common characteristics” (the second reading speech named key groups). A combination of intoxication and drug-induced psychosis has been held not to obviate a stated motivation to offend against people of a particular appearance. One case held the motive must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, consistent with the general rule for adverse facts (findings.formosa); there has been little judicial consideration of the provision.

refs.q: The Act does not identify – or limit – groups that share ‘common characteristics’, but the Attorney-General’s second reading speech did identify key groups the provision is designed to protect.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.5 – Hate crimes

refs.q: In another case, the court found that the fact an accused is acting under a combination of intoxication and a drug induced psychosis does not obviate their stated motivation to offend against people of dark-skinned appearance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.5 – Hate crimes

refs.q: In one case the court held that the existence of a hateful or prejudicial motive must be proved ‘beyond a reasonable doubt’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.5 – Hate crimes

title: Victim circumstances and harm: required by statute and common law
statement: Consideration of the victim’s circumstances is required by statute and the common law, and the Act requires the court to consider both the impact of the offence on the victim and any resulting injury, loss or damage (harm).

refs.q: This consideration of the victim’s circumstances is required by both statute and the common law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.6 – Impact on and circumstances of the victim

refs.q: The Act requires a court to consider both the impact of an offence on the victim and any resulting injury, damage, or loss (‘harm’).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.7 – Harm (direct injury, loss, or damage)

title: Surrounding circumstances; elements inform seriousness; uncharged injury in exposure offences
statement: The circumstances of an offence are not marked by neat lines at its technical beginning and end; surrounding circumstances directly related to it may be considered (it may be a question of degree). The elements of an offence help determine its seriousness and influenced the maximum. Considering a victim’s injury when sentencing for recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk, where no separate charge was brought for the injury, does not infringe the uncharged-conduct principle; but if the offender is separately sentenced for causing the injury, it cannot also be used for the exposure offence.

refs.q: Common-sense dictates that the circumstances of the offence are not marked out by neat lines marking the technical beginning and ending of a crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances

refs.q: The elements of an offence help determine its seriousness and influenced Parliament’s choice of maximum penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances

refs.q: It does not infringe that principle for a court consider the fact of a victim’s injury when sentencing for the offence of recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk where no separate charge was brought with respect to the injury.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.5 – Uncharged conduct and surrounding facts

refs.q: However, where an offender stands to be sentenced separately for causing injury, that conduct cannot be taken into account in sentencing for reckless exposure offence as that would involve double punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.5 – Uncharged conduct and surrounding facts

title: Family violence: stern punishment; context of control is not “merely background”
statement: Courts have a duty to protect vulnerable members of the community and will not hesitate to punish brutal and degrading abuse of a domestic partner sternly. The offending as a whole cannot be deconstructed to divorce individual charges from a context of degradation, control, threats and fear; conduct in an atmosphere of vitriol after a relationship breakdown is not merely background.

refs.q: Those considering the brutal and degrading abuse of a domestic partner must understand the courts have duty to protect vulnerable members of the community and will not hesitate to punish them sternly.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.3 – Family violence

refs.q: The offending as a whole cannot be deconstructed in order to divorce individual charges from a context of degradation, control, threats, and creating an environment of fear and dread.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.3 – Family violence

refs.q: For example, a person’s text messages may not constitute a direct attack against a former partner, but where they nonetheless take place ‘in an atmosphere of vitriol directed towards her, her children, and her new partner….in the wake of a relationship breakdown’ they are not ‘merely background’ to subsequent offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.3 – Family violence

title: Comparables: placing the case in a range; statistics showing an unjustified departure
statement: Sentencing requires the court to consider where the case fits within a range of seriousness. Appellate courts have received statistics clearly showing a sentence (or minimum term) outside the usual range where the departure had no evident justification.

cautions.text: Commonwealth offences only: practices for the same offences throughout Australia must be considered (outside this app’s Victorian scope).

refs.q: However, for Commonwealth offences, a court must have regard to sentencing practices for the same offences in other jurisdictions throughout Australia.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Sentencing requires a court to consider where the matter before it fits within a range of seriousness.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3 – Resources for determining current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.3.1 – Case comparisons

refs.q: Appellate courts have also received statistical material that clearly shows a sentence (or minimum term) is outside the usual range, and where that departure was made with no evident justification.
