title: Personal circumstances are needed to identify the purposes; gender-associated factors
statement: The sentencing purposes to be furthered cannot be identified without considering the offender’s personal circumstances. Although there can be no difference based solely on sex, the court need not disregard individual characteristics: factors closely associated with gender, such as pregnancy, may be considered.

refs.q: Identifying the sentencing purposes to be furthered in a case cannot be done if the court does not consider the personal circumstances of the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: But this does not mean a court must disregard the individual characteristics of an offender and treat a male offender as if they were female and vice-versa. In effect, this means that factors closely associated with gender, such as pregnancy, may be considered in appropriate circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

title: Verdins evidence: impact, not labels; proper expert opinion; rigorous assessment
statement: Verdins does not depend on diagnostic labels but on the impact of the impairment on the offender and their behaviour; it is generally not enough for an expert simply to describe the impairment. Expert evidence must be a legitimate expression of psychological opinion, without unsubstantiated conclusions outside the expert’s field (and experts may not opine on whether the Verdins principles apply). The court’s assessment must be rigorous and careful; the prosecution has an important part in identifying and challenging inadequacies.

refs.q: It is generally not sufficient for an expert to simply give evidence about the offender’s mental impairment. As noted, the Verdins principles do not depend on diagnostic labels, but on the impact of an impairment on the offender and the offender’s behaviour.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: It is wholly outside of a psychiatrist’s or psychologist’s expertise to express a view on whether one or more of the principles apply, and practitioners relying on expert reports should ensure they don’t contain impermissible opinions of that kind.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: Expert evidence presented to support a Verdins argument should be a ‘legitimate expression of psychological opinion’ and should not include ‘unsubstantiated conclusions on matters [falling] clearly outside any psychologist’s expertise’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: A court’s assessment of the evidence must be rigorous and careful, and the prosecution plays an important part in identifying and challenging any inadequacy in the expert’s opinion or the circumstances on which it is formed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

title: Prior and subsequent convictions: scope and proof
statement: The legislative list is not exclusive: “previous findings of guilt or convictions” are not only those before the offence being sentenced. Subsequent convictions cannot increase the head sentence; they may only counter an inference that the offender’s later conduct is mitigating. They are not proved through the Criminal Procedure Act provisions for tendering previous convictions; they may be placed before the court in submissions.

refs.q: The list of legislative considerations above is not exclusive: ‘previous findings of guilt or convictions’ does not refer only to those made or recorded prior to the commission of the offence currently before the court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: However, as with prior convictions, subsequent convictions cannot be used to increase the head sentence, but only to counter an inference that an offender’s later conduct was mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: ‘Subsequent convictions’ are not proved through the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) provisions on tendering an offender’s previous convictions.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: Instead, they may be placed before the court in the course of submissions.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

title: Bugmy: rigorous evaluation of the nexus
statement: Careful consideration must be given to whether the evidence establishes the required nexus between childhood deprivation and the offending: a rigorous evaluation, not a mechanical application in which a diagnostic label automatically invokes the specific application of Bugmy; a disadvantaged background alone attracts only the general application.

refs.q: Further, careful consideration needs to be given to whether the evidence establishes the required nexus. There must be a ‘rigorous evaluation of the evidence’ and not a mechanical application which permits a diagnostic label to automatically invoke the specific application of Bugmy.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: A disadvantaged background is not in itself sufficient to attract more than the general application of Bugmy.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

title: Why the offender’s circumstances matter
statement: Personal circumstances are a fundamental consideration that overlap with the offence. They identify which purposes matter (rehabilitation for a young offender; community protection and deterrence for a poor criminal history; reduced deterrence for compromised mental or intellectual capacity), may call for leniency (youth, advanced age, poor health, personal or family hardship) or severity (certain professions, parole or bail violators), and may engage statutory regimes (youth custody; targeted rehabilitative sanctions for serious drug addiction).

refs.q: The personal circumstances of an offender are a fundamental sentencing consideration. They are relevant in different ways and to multiple issues and frequently overlap with the circumstances of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Rehabilitation may be emphasised for a young offender, while protection of the community and deterrence may assume greater significance for an offender with a poor criminal history. Similarly, deterrence is likely to be of reduced value when sentencing an offender with compromised mental or intellectual capacity.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Independently of these considerations, an offender’s circumstances can also indicate the degree of lenience or severity called for in a particular case: youth, advanced age, poor health, or another personal or family hardship may call for leniency. By contrast, an offender’s status as a member of a certain profession, or as a parole or bail violator, may call for a more severe sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender

refs.q: Finally, an offender’s circumstances may be relevant to the applicability of particular statutory regimes: ‘young offenders’ may be sentenced to youth custody in place of adult imprisonment, and offenders with serious drug addictions may be appropriate candidates for targeted rehabilitative sanctions.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender

title: Advanced age (mature or elderly offenders)
statement: Age may mitigate where imprisonment may adversely affect an elderly offender’s health, the offender is less likely to be dangerous, more likely to die in prison (a larger proportion of remaining life), or imprisonment is more burdensome. Age is assessed at sentence (delay may make the offender older), but the effect of delay on the victim must be considered and a sentence is not moderated purely because delay made the offender older. Age is relevant to setting a minimum term and fixing the non-parole period. Weight depends on the circumstances; age never by itself excuses punishment; significant imprisonment may be appropriate for serious offences; just punishment, proportionality and deterrence remain primary. (Youth is dealt with by special statutory considerations: see purposes and youth orders.)

refs.q: imprisonment may adversely affect an elderly offender’s health;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

examples.text: less likely to be a danger

refs.q: the offender may be less likely to pose a danger to the community;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

examples.text: more likely to die in prison

refs.q: the offender may be more likely to die in prison and so any period of imprisonment will represent a larger proportion of their remaining life expectancy;

refs.q: imprisonment is likely to be more burdensome than on a younger offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

refs.q: There are also special statutory considerations that apply in sentencing a child or a ‘young offender’. This part looks only at sentencing mature or elderly offenders. Age may be a mitigating factor where:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

refs.q: A significant delay between offending and sentencing can also be relevant, because it means the offender is older than they would have been if sentenced closer to the offending, and it is the offender’s age at the time of sentencing that is relevant.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

refs.q: However, the effect of the delay on the victim must also be considered, and a sentence should not be moderated purely because the offender is significantly older as a result of delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

refs.q: Age is also relevant to determining whether to set a minimum term and in fixing any non-parole period.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

refs.q: The mitigating weight of age-based considerations depends on the circumstances of the case and other personal factors such as ill-health may be relevant. Age can never by itself excuse punishment. For serious offences, a significant period of imprisonment may be appropriate despite an offender’s advanced age. Just punishment, proportionality and deterrence always remain primary sentencing considerations, regardless of the offender’s age.
