refs.q: The age of an offender is a common law consideration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.1 – Age

title: Gender and gender identity
statement: Gender is largely irrelevant and there can be no difference based solely on sex, but closely associated factors (e.g. pregnancy) may be considered. For transgender offenders, associated factors (risk of harm in a facility, access to treatment) should be considered where appropriate; gender identity is not relevant to culpability, only to whether prison will be more onerous.

refs.q: An offender’s gender is largely irrelevant to sentencing, and there can be no difference in sentencing based solely on sex.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

refs.q: In effect, this means that factors closely associated with gender, such as pregnancy, may be considered in appropriate circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

refs.q: Transgender offenders also have closely associated factors, such as increased risk of harm in a specified facility, or the ability to access treatment, and these should be considered where appropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

refs.q: But this does not mean that gender identity is relevant to culpability, it is not. It is only relevant to the extent that prison will likely be more onerous for the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

refs.q: Nor is ‘gender’ limited to its traditional biological meaning.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.2 – Gender

title: Ethnicity, culture and race (no differential sentencing in themselves)
statement: Ethnicity, culture and race are not in themselves bases for differential sentencing, but associated considerations may be taken into account depending on their connection with the offence. Treating Aboriginal offenders as generally less culpable because of deprived background is racial stereotyping; an Aboriginal offender’s deprived background may mitigate to the same extent as a non-Aboriginal offender’s.

refs.q: Similarly, ethnicity, culture and race are not in themselves bases for differential sentencing, but they may be associated with considerations that can properly be taken into account where relevant and depending on their connection with the circumstances of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: to say that Aboriginal offenders are generally less culpable than a non-Aboriginal offender because of their deprived background is racial stereotyping of a kind that denies a ‘full measure of human dignity’ to Aboriginal people.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: However, an Aboriginal offender’s deprived background may be taken as a mitigating factor to the same extent as is the deprived background of a non-Aboriginal offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

title: Participation in a Koori Court sentencing conversation
statement: An Aboriginal offender’s participation in a Koori Court sentencing conversation may mitigate: participation is voluntary and may be confronting (being “shamed”); it may be used to demonstrate remorse and insight, express an intent to reform and explain how; and the genuineness of the offender’s statements matters.

refs.q: Moreover, an Aboriginal offender’s participation in a Koori Court sentencing conversation may be mitigating because of various factors, including:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: the fact that participation is voluntary and may be confronting for the offender as the result of their being ‘shamed’;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: whether the offender takes participation in the process as an opportunity to demonstrate remorse and insight into the seriousness and effect of the offending, express an intent to reform and explain how that will be done; and
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: the genuineness of the offender’s statements during the conversation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

title: Cultural norms
statement: The weight of a cultural norm is discretionary: if it obliged the offender or confined their choices (little or no choice), culpability may be diminished and rehabilitation viewed positively; if merely a justification, it does not. A norm may not outweigh the seriousness of the offending or the principles (so-called “honour killings” call for the strongest denunciation and increased general and specific deterrence); it cannot create a different range for a cultural group; and a bare assertion is not enough — it must be established by evidence relevant to the offender.

cautions.text: Commonwealth offences only: customary law and cultural practices cannot be used in aggravation or mitigation (outside this app’s Victorian scope).

refs.q: Lastly, it is important to note that when sentencing for Commonwealth offences, a court is specifically precluded from using customary law and cultural practices either in aggravation or mitigation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: More generally, the weight to be given to a cultural norm is a discretionary matter for the court informed by whether the norm obliged the offender to engage in the criminal conduct or confined their choices so as to diminish their moral culpability or was merely a justification for engaging in the criminal act(s).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: If the norm made the offender feel obligated, as if they had little or no choice but to engage in the conduct, their moral culpability may be diminished and their prospects of rehabilitation considered positively. If it was merely a justification it does not.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: However, a cultural norm may not be given such weight that it outweighs the seriousness of the offending or the sentencing principles.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: so-called ‘honour killings’ call for denunciation in the strongest possible terms and an increased need for general and specific deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: It also cannot give rise to a different range of sentences that are appropriate to an offender based on whether or not they are a member of a particular cultural group.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: Nor is a court required to act upon a simple assertion that cultural background affected the offending - it must be established by evidence relevant to the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: To describe the killing of another person in such a manner invests it with a wholly inappropriate degree of legitimacy; no civilised society can tolerate the killing of another person for such an amorphous concept as honour.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: In addition, the whole notion of an honour killing is based on a view of women as being merely the property of men, which has no place in this country.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

title: Physical health or disability
statement: Relevant where imprisonment will be a greater (6.2.1.1: “significantly more”) burden because of the offender’s health (ask whether ill health makes imprisonment more burdensome, not vice versa — e.g. dietary management, therapies, treatment), or there is a serious risk of imprisonment having a grave (6.2.1.2: “materially adverse”) effect on health; the Manual words the thresholds differently and the app applies neither as stricter (flag.physical_health_thresholds). Weight depends on the circumstances. Likely death within the sentence goes to burden but can never justify a manifestly inadequate sentence. No special rules for particular conditions; a condition alone is not mitigating — evidence must establish hardship in prison (prison may even improve health); without evidence the court may decline to discount. Lowered life expectancy may reduce the need for specific deterrence.

refs.q: The physical health or disability of the offender is relevant where: • imprisonment will be a greater burden because of their health; or • there is a serious risk of imprisonment having a grave effect on their health.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability

refs.q: Although mitigating, the weight given to these factors depends on the circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability

refs.q: Where imprisonment will be significantly more burdensome than for a person in normal health, this will be a circumstance of mitigation. A court must consider whether the offender’s ill health will make imprisonment a greater burden, not whether imprisonment will make the offender’s ill health a greater burden.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.1 – Increased burden of imprisonment

refs.q: The need for dietary management, physical therapies, and other courses of treatment within prison have been recognised as increasing the custodial burden.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.1 – Increased burden of imprisonment

refs.q: If the offender’s condition is likely to result in death within the period of sentence this goes to the burden of imprisonment, but the prospect that an offender may die in prison can never justify a manifestly inadequate sentence and all sentencing principles remain relevant.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.1 – Increased burden of imprisonment

refs.q: The second mitigating circumstance is where there is a serious risk of imprisonment having a materially adverse effect on the offender’s health.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.2 – Adverse effect on offender’s health

refs.q: There are no special rules for particular illnesses or disabilities, and each case should be decided according to its own circumstances. The presence of a condition does not on its own immediately constitute a mitigating factor. The evidence must establish that an offender will suffer hardship in prison as a result of their illness, especially as there may be some instances where imprisonment may actually improve the offender’s health.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

refs.q: Where no evidence is led, a court may decline to discount sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

refs.q: An offender’s ill-health may also be relevant to the sentencing principles because of the likelihood that the person has a lowered life expectancy may reduce the need for specific deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

refs.q: This often takes the form of a more rapid progression of the disease from the circumstances of incarceration, such as stress adding further complications to a pre-existing condition.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.2 – Adverse effect on offender’s health

title: Worsening prognosis after sentence; injuries as extra-curial punishment
statement: A substantially worse prognosis after a health-based reduction may be led on appeal as fresh evidence, but where offending is serious and imprisonment beyond life expectancy was expected, the prognosis is a matter for the Executive (prerogative of mercy). Injuries sustained during offending or in custody may be extra-curial punishment, relevant to the choice of sanction and the length of imprisonment.

refs.q: If a court reduces sentence because of the offender’s health, but their prognosis subsequently becomes substantially worse, evidence of that changed situation may be led on appeal as fresh evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

refs.q: But where the offending is serious, imprisonment beyond life expectancy was expected, and there is no chance that period will be reduced on appeal, the offender’s condition and prognosis are instead a matter for the Executive to consider in the exercise of the prerogative of mercy rather than a basis to re-open the sentencing discretion.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

refs.q: Injuries sustained during offending or while in custody may also be considered as ‘extra-curial punishment’. These injuries can be relevant in two ways: first, with respect to the choice of sanction, and second, they may dictate the length of any term of imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability > 6.2.1.3 – Generally

title: Impaired mental functioning (Verdins): the six ways it is relevant
statement: The court must take into account impaired mental or intellectual functioning of any cause, permanence, severity or duration, existing at offending or sentence. Labels do not matter: what matters is the evidence of the nature, extent and effect of the impairment at the relevant time. Six (non-exhaustive) ways it may be relevant (limbs below); the nature and degree of a relevant impairment may differ from one aspect to another, so it is assessed limb by limb. The considerations may moderate both head sentence and minimum term, but are exceptional, should not be invoked in routine cases, and need not be recited as a checklist.

limbs.text: reduced moral culpability → affects just punishment, less denunciation

refs.q: It may reduce an offender’s moral culpability and so affect what is considered to be a just punishment and lessen the need for denunciation;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

limbs.text: kind of sentence and conditions of service

refs.q: It may have a bearing on the kind of sentence that is imposed and the conditions under which it should be served;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated as a consideration depending on the nature and severity of the offender’s symptoms, and the effect of their impairment at the time of offending, sentence, or both;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: Specific deterrence may be similarly moderated or eliminated in the same circumstances;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: The existence of an impairment at the time of sentencing, or its reasonably foreseeable reoccurrence, may mean that a specific sentence may weigh more heavily on the offender than it would on a person in normal health;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

limbs.text: serious risk of significant adverse impact on mental health

refs.q: If there is a serious risk that imprisonment will have a significantly adverse impact on the offender’s mental health, this will be a mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: A court must take into account an offender’s impaired mental or intellectual functioning – whether it be the result of illness, injury, disability, or disorder, whether permanent or temporary, mild or severe, newly acquired or longstanding and whether the impairment existed at the time of the offending or at the time of sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: The Verdins principles do not depend on diagnostic labels: ‘What matters is what the evidence shows about the nature, extent and effect of the mental impairment experienced by the offender at the relevant time’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: Specifically, how did it affect them at the time of the offending or how is it likely to impact their experience of imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: In R v Verdins (‘Verdins’), the Court of Appeal identified six ways that mental impairment may be relevant to sentencing:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: These Verdins ‘principles’ or ‘considerations’ may moderate both the minimum term and the head sentence, but they are exceptional and should not be invoked in routine cases. Lastly, a court is not required to run through and recite all of the Verdins principles as though exhausting a checklist.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)

refs.q: The Verdins principles are six different, non-exhaustive, aspects of sentencing, so the nature and degree of a relevant impairment may be different depending on which aspect of the process is under consideration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

title: Verdins limb 1: moral culpability
statement: Culpability may be reduced if, at the time of the offence, the impairment reduced the ability to exercise judgment, make calm and rational choices, think clearly or appreciate wrongfulness; disinhibited the offender; obscured intent; or contributed causally (a descriptive, non-exhaustive list). It is a matter of degree assessed with expert evidence and the offender’s conduct before, during and after: did the impairment make the offender less blameworthy? A causal connection is not required but some connection is: a “realistic connection”, or the impairment “caused or contributed to” or was “causally linked” to the offending (flag.verdins_connection_test). For serious offences, or where the offender knew the nature, gravity and wrongfulness of the conduct (indicated by planning and avoiding detection), the reduction may be minor or limited (the Manual notes contrary authority on the latter: fn 1151). Both Verdins and Bugmy allow culpability to be viewed as reduced; expert evidence is required to show how the two are connected and, where they converge, inappropriate double counting is avoided, but Bugmy is considered in its own right.

refs.q: The first Verdins principle says that if a mentally impaired offender is less morally culpable for their actions then it may not be appropriate to punish them as harshly as someone who is fully responsible.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: reduced their ability to exercise appropriate judgment, make calm and rational choices, think clearly, or appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct; or • made them disinhibited; or • obscured the intent to commit the offence; or • contributed causally to the commission of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: This is not an exhaustive list - it is descriptive rather than prescriptive.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: The effect of an impairment on moral culpability is a matter of degree. A court should consider the gravity of the offending and, with the assistance of any expert evidence, the offender’s conduct before, during, and after the offending in order to determine the extent of the impairment’s contribution to the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: The relevant question is whether the evidence establishes that the impairment contributed in a way that made the offender ‘less blameworthy as a result’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: This is a discretionary assessment with no fixed guidelines, although the High Court has said that there will usually be such a link if the offender is intellectually disabled.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: While a causal connection is not required by Verdins to reduce the offender’s culpability (or to moderate or eliminate general and specific deterrence), some connection is still required. If the impairment existed at the time of the offending there must be a ‘realistic connection’ between the two, or the impairment must have ‘caused or contributed to’ or be ‘causally linked’ to the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: If the offence is serious, an offender’s culpability may only be reduced to a minor extent, even if their impairment is significant. Similarly, culpability may only be reduced to a limited extent where the offender was fully aware of the nature and gravity of what they were doing, and that it was wrong. Planning and management of the offending and avoiding detection are indicative of such knowledge.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: But it will require expert evidence to show how the two are connected, and if there is convergence between the two care should be taken to avoid ‘inappropriate double counting’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: ‘[T]he principles identified in Bugmy must be considered in their own right quite apart from the impact of any mental impairment pursuant to Verdins principles’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: A common feature of both Verdins and Bugmy principles is that both permit a court to view the offender’s moral culpability as being reduced where their psychological functioning or personality structure has been impaired.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: But see Howell 357 [23].
An offender’s moral culpability may be reduced if, at the time of the offence, their impairment:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: As noted, one way that moral culpability may be reduced is where there is a causal connection between the offender’s impairment and the offending conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

title: Verdins limb 2: type of sentence and conditions
statement: Impairment may make some sanctions (e.g. imprisonment where the impairment is significantly impacted or treatment is unavailable) inappropriate; specific statutory sanctions and custodial alternatives exist for impaired offenders. But limb 2 does not mean imprisonment cannot be imposed; the court considers the possibility on the facts.

refs.q: An offender’s impairment may be relevant to the type of sanction imposed. It may make some sanctions – such as imprisonment, where the offender’s mental impairment is significantly impacted, or they are unable to obtain treatment – inappropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.3 – Type of sentence and conditions

refs.q: There are specific statutory sanctions that are appropriate for offenders who are mentally impaired, as well as alternatives to custodial terms that can be imposed for those offenders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.3 – Type of sentence and conditions

refs.q: However, while an offender’s impairment may be relevant to the kind of sentence imposed, the second Verdins principle does not say that a term of imprisonment cannot be imposed. It requires a court to consider the possibility by reference to the facts and circumstances of the case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.3 – Type of sentence and conditions

title: Verdins limb 3: general deterrence
statement: General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated, but not automatically: it depends on the severity and nature of the condition and its effect on mental capacity at offending, sentence or both, and generally some (possibly causal) connection with the offending. There must be an evidentiary basis and “proper and informed” consideration of how the impairment materially diminished the capacity to reason about wrongfulness, or why full general deterrence would be repugnant to humanitarian considerations. An offender may not be an “appropriate vehicle” (a causal relationship is usually sufficient, although this may not apply if the offender acted knowing the conduct was wrong). Extent depends on symptoms, effect on capacity, and the nature and gravity of the offence. It is relatively clear that general deterrence will be wholly eliminated in the most extreme cases (where a mental impairment defence might have been established); it is not moderated where the impairment arose as a reaction to discovery or the prospect of prison; each case is decided on its facts.

refs.q: General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated if an offender suffers from an impairment at the time of offending, sentencing, or both. But Verdins does not automatically require that general deterrence be modified where a person’s mental functioning is impaired.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: The question is whether it should be moderated and that will depend on both the severity and nature of the condition and its effect on the offender’s mental capacity at the time of offending, sentencing, or both. Generally, this means that some connection, which may be causal, between mental condition and the offending is required.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: Further, there must be an evidentiary basis to moderate general deterrence. It is not sufficient to find that an offender suffers from a mental impairment. There must be ‘proper and informed’ consideration of how the impairment materially diminished the offender’s capacity to reason appropriately about the wrongfulness of their conduct at the time of the offending, or how the offender’s condition might make full application of the principles of general deterrence repugnant to the humanitarian considerations that guide proper sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: Another consideration is whether the offender is an ‘appropriate vehicle’ for general deterrence. This may be determined by looking at whether the offender’s impairment would evoke the community’s sympathy and make people wonder why the offender is being punished. A causal relationship between the impairment and the offending is usually sufficient to find that an offender is not an appropriate vehicle for general deterrence. Although, this may not apply if the offender acted knowing that their conduct was wrong.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: The extent to which an impairment will moderate or eliminate general deterrence depends on three factors: • the nature and severity of the symptoms exhibited by the offender; • the effect of the condition on the mental capacity of the offender; and • the nature and gravity of the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: It is relatively clear that general deterrence will be wholly eliminated in the most extreme cases, such as where an offender might have established a substantive defence of mental impairment. It is also clear that general deterrence should not be moderated where the offender’s mental impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of their crimes or the prospect of incarceration. Ultimately, however, each case must be decided on its facts.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

title: Verdins limb 4: specific deterrence
statement: Specific deterrence may be harder to achieve and often not worth pursuing for an impaired offender; it has little relevance where the impairment prevents acceptance of responsibility, but is relevant if the offender can appreciate wrongfulness. Not moderated where the impairment is a reaction to discovery or the prospect of prison, or where imprisonment will in fact deter despite the impairment.

refs.q: However, if the offender suffers from a mental impairment, ‘specific deterrence may be more difficult to achieve and is often not worth pursuing’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Whether and to what degree specific deterrence applies to an impaired offender depends on the circumstances. Where the impairment makes them unable to accept their role in and responsibility for the offending, specific deterrence has little relevance. But if an offender is able to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct, specific deterrence is relevant.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Specific deterrence should also not be moderated where the offender’s mental impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of their crimes or the prospect of incarceration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: Nor should it be moderated or eliminated if the court finds that imprisonment will actually have a specifically deterrent effect notwithstanding the offender’s impairment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: One of the purposes of punishment is to specifically deter the offender from re-offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

refs.q: This assumes the offender is capable of learning from the experience of punishment and can therefore be deterred from repeating the same or similar conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence

title: Verdins limbs 5 and 6: heavier burden; serious risk to mental health
statement: Limb 5: a significant additional burden must be shown, considering the nature of custody (isolation, protection, circumscribed conditions, unavailable treatment). Limb 6: a serious risk of a significantly adverse effect on mental health beyond the deterioration imprisonment causes anyone, assessed by illness history, likely conditions, management difficulties and likelihood and effectiveness of treatment. For these limbs it does not matter that the impairment arose on discovery or because of the prospect of prison. Impairment alone, or stress at the prospect of prison, is not enough; the defence must establish the likely effect; without evidence no moderation is needed, though the court may infer greater burden for a severe condition depending on the totality of the evidence (flag.verdins_expert_evidence_normally_vs_required). Weight varies and does not displace the other purposes.

refs.q: Firstly, imprisonment may weigh more heavily on an impaired offender than it would a person in normal health. But in order to mitigate sentence on this basis it must be shown the impaired offender will suffer a significant additional burden. In determining this, a court should consider the nature of the custody.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: The burden of incarceration may be increased if the offender’s term will be served in isolation, protective custody, or under other circumscribed conditions, or if the offender’s custodial placements are limited by the unavailability of appropriate treatment regimes.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: Secondly, a sentence should be mitigated if there is a ‘serious risk’ imprisonment will have a ‘significantly adverse effect’ on an offender’s mental health. The deterioration that is likely to be caused by imprisonment must be greater than the mental deterioration that imprisonment generally causes any person to suffer.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: In assessing the risk, a court should consider the history of the offender’s illness, the likely conditions of imprisonment, any difficulties in management presented by the offender, and the likelihood of the offender receiving treatment (and its effectiveness) while imprisoned.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: In either case, it does not matter that an offender’s mental impairment arose because their crimes were discovered or due to the prospect of incarceration. If their condition is likely to be aggravated by the experience of imprisonment, a court may reduce the offender’s sentence. However, the weight to be given to these considerations always varies and does not displace consideration of the other sentencing purposes in the instinctive synthesis.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: The existence of the impairment alone or stress at the prospect of a prison term is not sufficient to mitigate the sentence. The defence must establish the likely effect the offender’s impairment will have on the offender’s experience of imprisonment. Where there is no evidence that prison would be more burdensome for the offender, or may worsen their condition, there is no need to moderate sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: It is open for the court to infer, in the absence of direct evidence, that a prisoner who suffers from a severe mental health condition would find prison more burdensome than another prisoner in normal health. However, whether that inference should be drawn depends on the totality of the evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: Fresh evidence that an offender’s condition has deteriorated to a much greater degree than anticipated by the sentencing court may be admissible on appeal.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

refs.q: The consequences of imprisonment are relevant in sentencing a mentally impaired offender in two ways.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment

title: Mental impairment and community protection
statement: Impairment may reduce culpability but make the offender a danger, increasing the importance of community protection — also where there is a significant record, or the offender knew stopping medication or substance abuse risked reoffending or violence. For a “serious offender”, community protection is the principal purpose despite impairment; but no single consideration should exclude the others.

refs.q: An offender’s mental impairment may reduce their culpability for an offence, but it may also make them a danger to society thereby increasing the importance of community protection as a sentencing consideration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.7 – Community protection

refs.q: Community protection is also important where an impaired offender has a significant criminal record, or they understood that in stopping their medication there was a risk they would reoffend having done so previously, or that substance abuse would lead to violent behaviour and yet continued to indulge.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.7 – Community protection

refs.q: Where the offender is sentenced as a ‘serious offender’, the court must regard protection of the community as the principal sentencing purpose, despite the existence of a mental impairment. But, as always, although community protection may be a key sentencing consideration, a court should not focus on one consideration to the exclusion of other relevant factors.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.7 – Community protection

title: Mental impairment and rehabilitation (shorter non-parole period)
statement: Impairment is relevant to rehabilitation prospects and may make rehabilitation primary where punishment, denunciation and deterrence need little emphasis; the court may set a shorter than usual non-parole period so treatment can start earlier, particularly where the impairment cannot be treated or managed in prison.

refs.q: Mental impairment is relevant to the extent that it bears upon an offender’s prospects for rehabilitation. It may also make rehabilitation the primary consideration where the other purposes (such as punishment, denunciation and deterrence) do not require significant emphasis because of the offender’s impairment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.8 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: In such cases, a court may emphasise rehabilitation by setting a shorter than usual non-parole period so that treatment can be carried out at an earlier stage than usual.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.8 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: This course might be appropriate where the offender’s impairment cannot be properly treated or managed in a prison environment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.8 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: The relevant authorities may then also monitor the offender’s condition for a longer period of time once they are returned to the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.8 – Rehabilitation

title: Self-induced impairment, substance abuse and relapse
statement: Mitigation may be reduced where the condition is self-induced (drugs, alcohol): the key is foreknowledge that the substance was likely to produce a delusional state. A history of using substances known to cause hallucinations and violence means culpability is unlikely to be reduced and use may aggravate. If impairment and substance abuse are independent, Verdins applies with full force. If the impairment caused the substance abuse, culpability and deterrence may be moderated, but the defence must still prove a connection between impairment and offending (drug quantity may be considered). A relapse caused by not taking medication or by illegal drugs is not mitigating, although moral culpability may still be reduced if another factor beyond the offender’s control (e.g. significant stress from a relationship breakdown or personal loss) also played some part.

refs.q: The mitigatory effect of mental impairment may be reduced where the condition is self-induced, often by drug or alcohol use. The key issue is what the offender knew about the possible consequences of taking the relevant substance, what is required is foreknowledge that use of a substance ‘was likely to produce a delusional state’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse

refs.q: An offender’s culpability is unlikely to be reduced where they have a history of using substances known to lead to hallucinations and violence. Indeed, use of substances in that situation may be an aggravating factor.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse

refs.q: However, where the offender’s mental impairment and substance abuse are independent, the Verdins principles will continue to have full force, meaning the considerations of denunciation and deterrence (general and specific) will have little role to play.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse

refs.q: Similarly, where the substance abuse is caused by the offender’s impairment, their moral culpability may be reduced, and the need for general and specific deterrence may be moderated. But it is not enough to establish the impairment led to substance abuse. The defence must still prove that the impairment was connected to the offending. In determining whether drug use was caused by an impairment, the court may take into account the quantity of drugs used.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse

refs.q: An offender cannot rely on a relapse of a pre-existing mental impairment as mitigating if it is caused by their failing to take prescribed medication or ingesting illegal drugs, but their moral culpability may still be reduced if another factor beyond their control - such as significant stress from the breakdown of a relationship or personal loss - also played some part in their relapse into a mentally impaired state.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse

title: Personality disorders under Verdins
statement: Verdins applies to personality disorders like any other condition (no blanket exclusion), but a disorder does not necessarily show impaired functioning; what matters is what the expert evidence shows about its effect on mental functioning at the offending or in future. Contrary statements in DPP v O’Neill should not be followed.

refs.q: The Verdins principles apply to personality disorders as they do to any other condition, there is no blanket exclusion of them from that framework. But neither does the existence of such a disorder necessarily demonstrate impaired mental functioning.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.10 – Personality disorders

refs.q: The question of whether an offender’s personality disorder engages any of the Verdins principles does not depend on its particular diagnostic label, but on what the expert evidence before the court shows about how the condition affected the offender’s mental functioning at the time of the offending or how it will do so in the future.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.10 – Personality disorders

refs.q: An offender with a diagnosed personality disorder stands in precisely the same position as any other offender who wishes to rely on impaired mental functioning in order to mitigate their sentence in one or more of the ways identified by Verdins, and any statement to the contrary in DPP (Vic) v O’Neill should not be followed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.10 – Personality disorders

use: intake asks whether expert evidence exists; auditor flags Verdins reasoning without an evidentiary basis
title: Verdins: raising it, evidence and reasons
statement: Generally, Verdins need only be considered if clearly raised and supported by sufficient evidence; the defence must adduce it and the court need not inquire (save where a link is shown and the inference is the only one reasonably open). It is wrong to assume Verdins applies because an impairment exists: rigorous consideration of which limbs apply is required. Cogent, normally expert, evidence must establish on the balance of probabilities the impairment at the relevant time and its nature, extent and effect, assessed against the offence facts (the Manual also says expert evidence “is required” but not determinative: flag.verdins_expert_evidence_normally_vs_required). Experts must not opine on whether the principles apply — that is for the court. Be cautious; imprecise opinions make firm findings difficult; self-reported and uncorroborated reports may be rejected. If not accepting uncontested expert evidence, give notice and an opportunity to be heard. Reasons must explain how the impairment was taken into account (or why Verdins was rejected).

refs.q: Generally, a court only needs to consider the Verdins principles in cases where the issue is clearly raised by counsel, and there is a sufficient evidentiary basis to do so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: Defence counsel must submit evidence supporting a Verdins point advanced in mitigation, particularly when the court indicates that it is unpersuaded by their submissions. A court does not have an obligation to inquire into the evidence or to make a factual inference about a mental impairment (unless there was a link between the impairment and the crime and a factual inference was the only conclusion reasonably open).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: Similarly, there is no obligation for a court to consider the Verdins principles where defence counsel mentions the principles, but later retreats from reliance on them.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: It is mechanistic, simplistic, and wrong to say that because an offender suffers from a mental impairment the Verdins principles apply. There has to be a careful and rigorous consideration of whether the evidence establishes that the offender’s mental capacity has been impaired and which of the circumstances identified in Verdins are applicable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: There needs to be cogent evidence, normally in the form of expert evidence, establishing on the balance of the probabilities that the Verdins principles are enlivened. The evidence must establish that the impairment existed at the time of offending, sentence, or both, as well as its nature, extent, and effect on the offender or its likely effect on them in the future. Expert evidence also needs to be assessed against what is known about the circumstances of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: While expert evidence is required, it is not determinative, and it is ultimately for the court, not a psychiatrist or psychologist, to decide if and how the Verdins principles apply in a given case. It is wholly outside of a psychiatrist’s or psychologist’s expertise to express a view on whether one or more of the principles apply, and practitioners relying on expert reports should ensure they don’t contain impermissible opinions of that kind.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: A court should be cautious before concluding that an offender suffered from a mental impairment at the relevant time, and that the impairment had one of the necessary effects. Imprecision in expert opinions should signal to the court that it will be difficult to make a firm conclusion on their findings.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: If a court is not inclined to accept the uncontested evidence of an expert, or to only give it limited weight because the author of an expert report is not called to give evidence, it must give counsel notice of this and an opportunity to be heard.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: As the Court of Appeal has noted, because many expert reports are self-serving and almost always based on self-reported information, a court has an obligation to carefully consider this evidence and must exercise great caution in determining if Verdins has been enlivened. Thus, a court may reject an uncorroborated expert report based on self-reported information, particularly if the report writer believes the offender was lying.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: If the court accepts the evidence and concludes that one or more of the Verdins principles apply, its reasons should clearly explain the ways the impairment has been taken into account. It is not sufficient to merely refer to the competing submissions, or state that the offender’s impaired mental functioning affected the sentence without explaining how or to what extent. Similarly, if a court concludes the evidence is inadequate to support an expert opinion and rejects an application of Verdins it must state its reasons for reaching that conclusion.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: Moreover, an impairment may have subtle abnormalities that affect perception and conduct and expert evidence on those subtleties will assist.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

title: Addiction (gambling, drugs, alcohol)
statement: Addiction may bear on culpability (e.g. trafficking to feed one’s own addiction rather than greed), but that weight is greatly diminished, often to nothing, above street level; advantaged background, manner of involvement and intended use may lessen mitigation. Importation is inferred to be for profit absent evidence; needing money for a debt does not affect culpability; good character carries less weight in importation. Addiction is relevant to rehabilitation, deterrence and community protection, but someone with repeated opportunities for reform should not expect to rely on it. It may bear on choice of sanction (tailored or rehabilitative sanctions). Addiction does not require a conclusion that culpability is lessened.

cautions.text: If the lack of an addiction is used to show the offender acted solely from greed, the absence of addiction must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

refs.q: If the lack of an addiction is to be used to prove the offender acted solely from greed, then proof (beyond a reasonable doubt) that they are not addicted is required.

cautions.text: Addiction does not require a finding that moral culpability is lessened.

refs.q: But it does not require a conclusion that moral culpability is lessened.
Addictions, such as gambling addiction, drug addiction or alcoholism, can be relevant in several ways.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Firstly, addiction may bear on an offender’s moral culpability. For example, it is relevant if the offender trafficked drugs in order to feed their own addiction rather than purely from greed and for profit. But the weight to be attributed to this fact depends on the circumstances of each case and is greatly diminished, often to the point of non-existence, when considering trafficking operations above street level.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Similarly, an offender’s advantaged background, the way they were involved in a trafficking scheme, how they attempted to obtain a drug, and what they intended to do with it are all relevant to determining their culpability and may lessen any mitigating impact.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Moreover, unless there is evidence to the contrary, it should be inferred that a person importing drugs is doing so for profit. The fact that an offender needs money to pay off a debt does not affect culpability, and their prior good character is given less weight in drug importation offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Secondly, addiction is also relevant to rehabilitation, deterrence and community protection. However, someone who has had repeated opportunities for reform should not reasonably expect to rely on addiction in mitigation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Lastly, an offender’s addiction may be relevant to the choice of sanction, either because it may qualify them for a sanction specifically tailored to their addiction or by emphasising the value of a general rehabilitative sanction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

note: direction “either”: rarely mitigating (only in quite exceptional circumstances) and may aggravate
title: Intoxication (rarely mitigating; may aggravate)
statement: Intoxication rarely mitigates and may aggravate; to reduce culpability the circumstances must be “quite exceptional”. The key is foreknowledge: knowing the likely consequences increases culpability. A long history of drinking without any indication of violence may make the circumstances exceptional enough to mitigate. Intoxication may also be relevant to remorse and rehabilitation.

refs.q: Intoxication – whether through alcohol or narcotic consumption – will rarely mitigate offending, and may even be an aggravating factor. For intoxication to reduce moral culpability, the circumstances will have to be ‘quite exceptional’. The key question is the degree of foreknowledge. If the offender knew of the likely consequences of drug ingestion their culpability is increased, and intoxication may be an aggravating factor. Where a long history of alcohol consumption has not revealed the slightest indication that an offender poses a risk of violence, this may mean the circumstances are sufficiently exceptional to be mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.4 – Intoxication

refs.q: And as with addiction, intoxication may be relevant to sentencing purposes such as remorse and rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.4 – Intoxication

note: jurisdiction mixed: the second ref also states the Commonwealth position (recognizance release orders); the statement is limited to the Victorian uses
title: Character, past history and antecedents
statement: Character (synonymous with past history and antecedents) includes at least prior criminal history. It must be considered in determining sentence, whether to record a conviction, and fixing a non-parole period. The court may consider the number, seriousness, date, relevance and nature of prior findings of guilt or convictions; general reputation; and significant contributions to the community.

refs.q: ‘Character’, ‘past history’, and ‘antecedents’ have been used synonymously and refer (at a minimum) to an offender’s previous criminal history.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character

refs.q: Under both the Victorian and Commonwealth regimes consideration of an offender’s character is required when determining the sentence to be imposed, when deciding whether to exercise the discretion to record a State conviction, and when fixing a non-parole period or making a recognizance release order.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character

refs.q: the number, seriousness, date, relevance and nature of any previous findings of guilt or convictions; • their general reputation; and • any significant contributions they’ve made to the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character

refs.q: In determining an offender’s character, a court may consider:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character

title: Good character
statement: Good character is an established mitigating factor assessed apart from the current offending (“otherwise of good character”) and, subject to a statutory exception, must be taken into account; weight varies and the court may consider the nature of the offending when weighing it. A lack of similar priors is significant mitigation; good character always earns some (possibly minimal) leniency, balanced against the offence and purposes, depending on seriousness and whether isolated or a course of conduct (less weight for multiple offences). Significant for first offenders (especially mature ones or those under extraordinary external pressure), qualified by gravity, and relevant to rehabilitation. Reduced significance for offences commonly committed by people of good character or where respectability was exploited.

cautions.text: Child sexual offences: previous good character cannot be considered if the court is satisfied that it helped the offender commit the offence (statutory exception; a finding of fact).

refs.q: Further, in sentencing for a child sexual offence, a court cannot consider an offender’s previous good character if the court is satisfied that their good character helped them commit the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

cautions.text: Breach of trust goes to the weight of good character but cannot be used both to aggravate and to diminish good character.

refs.q: Factors such as breach of trust will similarly go to the weight to be given to the offender’s ‘otherwise good character’. But undue weight cannot be given to an offender’s breach of trust. It cannot be used both as an aggravating factor and to diminish an offender’s good character.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

cautions.text: Less weight in drug importation.

refs.q: their prior good character is given less weight in drug importation offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

cautions.text: The Court of Appeal has treated too much weight on good character in white collar crime and culpable driving as an error of past practice.

refs.q: a category of offenders had been persistently treated erroneously, with too much weight being given to mitigating factors (for example, too much weight being ascribed to good character in the case of those sentenced for white collar crimes or culpable driving); or
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.9 – Current sentencing practices > 5.2.9.2 – Changes to current sentencing practices

refs.q: Good character is an established mitigating factor, but what makes a person of good character varies according to the individual and it impossible to state a universal rule.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: In determining whether an offender is of good character, a court must not consider the offending for which it is sentencing the offender. The issue at sentencing is whether, apart from the current offending, the person is otherwise of good character.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: If the evidence establishes that the offender is ‘otherwise of good character’ then, subject to a statutory exception, this must be taken into account in sentencing. However, the weight given to good character will vary according to the circumstances of the case and the offender, and in determining the weight to be given to previous good character there is no prohibition on a court considering the nature and circumstances of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: A lack of similar prior convictions is 'a significant matter in mitigation'.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: An offender’s prior good character will always entitle them to some leniency, although it may be minimal. Good character must be balanced against the circumstances of the offence and the sentencing purposes. The weight to be given to good character may depend on the seriousness of the offence and whether it was an isolated act or part of a course of conduct. In the case of an offender charged with multiple offences the sentencer may attach less weight to previous good character.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: Good character is significant in cases of first offenders, particularly mature first offenders or those acting under extraordinary external pressures. But, again, this is qualified by the gravity of the offending and the other sentencing purposes.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: Good character is also relevant to an offender’s prospects of rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: Good character will be of reduced significance for offences that are commonly committed by offenders of otherwise good character, or who exploit their respectability to further their offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

title: Bad character: prior and subsequent convictions cannot increase the sentence
statement: Prior criminality is relevant but cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish; it may indicate moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or propensity and so inhibit mitigation such as rehabilitation. Subsequent convictions likewise cannot increase the head sentence or aggravate; they may only rebut claimed mitigation. The defence need not disclose subsequent convictions unless relying on good character; the prosecution must prove later convictions and relevant subsequent conduct whenever a non-parole period may be fixed. Rehabilitation between offending and sentence may reduce the negative impact of bad character.

refs.q: Evidence of an offender’s bad character, i.e., their prior criminality, is also relevant to a court in exercising the sentencing discretion, but it cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish an offender. Instead, it may indicate an offender’s moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or a propensity to commit particular crimes and so inhibit consideration of mitigatory factors such as rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: However, as with prior convictions, subsequent convictions cannot be used to increase the head sentence, but only to counter an inference that an offender’s later conduct was mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: Subsequent convictions recorded after the commission of the offence before the court are also relevant, but again cannot be considered to aggravate an offence and can only be considered for the purpose of rebutting alleged circumstances of mitigation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: The defence has no duty to inform the court of subsequent convictions, unless relying on the offender’s good character, but the prosecution has a duty to prove later convictions and other relevant subsequent conduct whenever it is open to the court to fix a non-parole period.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

refs.q: Lastly, if there is evidence of rehabilitation subsequent to the offending and prior to sentencing, then bad character may have a reduced negative impact.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character

title: Motive
statement: Motive may aggravate or mitigate depending on the circumstances. Lessening: genuine (not false) altruism; addiction without profit motive; personal or financial pressure or need; threats short of duress. Aggravating: misguided loyalty; greed or profit; status, self-aggrandisement or a lavish lifestyle; vigilantism; revenge, spite or dislike.

refs.q: genuine altruism, as opposed to ‘false’ altruism;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: addiction linked to offending with no profit motive;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: personal or financial pressures or need;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: threats falling short of the defence of duress.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: misguided loyalty;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: greed or profit;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: a desire for status, self-aggrandisement or to fund a lavish lifestyle;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: vigilantism, the law does not condone revenge or an offender punishing the victim;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: revenge, spite, or dislike.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive

refs.q: An offender’s motive may be considered in assessing their culpability. It may be an aggravating or mitigating factor, and the weight it is to be given depends on the circumstances.

refs.q: Culpability may be lessened if the offending was motivated by:

title: Childhood deprivation and disadvantage (Bugmy)
statement: Childhood deprivation or violence must be considered: its effects do not diminish with time and can explain but not excuse offending. Significant circumstances include family violence or abuse, addicted or alcoholic carers, educational disadvantage, sexual abuse, separation from natural parents, and severe persecution or refugee experience. It is an error to require the offender to demonstrate “significant childhood deprivation”, and it need not be “profound”; the Manual elsewhere speaks of “extreme disadvantage” (6.3.3) and of “significant deprivation” in the general expression’s rationale, so no threshold label is applied (flag.bugmy_degree_of_deprivation). It is also relevant in applying the fundamental principles and purposes. The court should make clear how the background moderated the weight given to purposes or principles and evaluate its extent. Mitigation must at some point yield to serious violent offending and community protection, particularly domestic violence. A disadvantaged upbringing may elevate rehabilitation and the need to avoid or minimise incarceration.
