title: Bugmy: general expression (inferred) versus specific expression (nexus by evidence)
statement: General expression: childhood deprivation may reduce culpability and can be inferred from the simple fact of deprivation, with no causal connection required. Specific expression: extreme deprivation explaining recourse to violence when frustrated may substantially reduce culpability, but requires a nexus between the deprivation and the inability to control the relevant impulse, a causal connection established by an appropriate evidentiary foundation and rigorous evaluation (not a diagnostic label). The nexus cannot be inferred from judicial experience or common sense; it is difficult to envisage sufficient evidence without a professional reasoned opinion.

refs.q: Lastly, it is important to distinguish the way in which deprivation is being considered and what must support that consideration. Bugmy said: 1) that an offender’s circumstances of childhood deprivation may mitigate their sentence because their moral culpability is likely to be less than one who was not so exposed, and 2) that an offender’s extreme deprivation may explain their recourse to violence when frustrated, to the extent that their moral culpability may be substantially reduced.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: Hermann has characterised the first of these as being the “general expression” of the relevance of childhood deprivation, and the second as being the "specific expression".
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has further said that the general expression can be inferred from the simple fact of deprivation; there is no requirement to establish a causal connection between the background and the offending because a background of significant deprivation is likely to leave an indelible mark and so will generally lessen an offender’s culpability.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: However, the second expression requires a nexus between childhood deprivation and the inability to control an impulse relevant to the offending conduct before it can substantially reduce an offender’s culpability. It must be established that the childhood experience does explain the offending conduct, at least in part. There must be a causal connection, established by an appropriate evidentiary foundation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: There must be a ‘rigorous evaluation of the evidence’ and not a mechanical application which permits a diagnostic label to automatically invoke the specific application of Bugmy.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: A disadvantaged background is not in itself sufficient to attract more than the general application of Bugmy. There must be a specific evidentiary foundation, which establishes and explains the relevant nexus, to invoke the specific application. The nexus cannot be inferred from judicial or other experience, or common sense.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: The evidence must be evaluated carefully, and while an expert psychological or psychiatric report may not be required in every case, the Court has clearly stated that it is difficult to envision a case where the evidentiary basis for a specific application of the Bugmy principles will be sufficiently strong in the absence of a “professional reasoned opinion”.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

title: Employment history; offending by those in government and justice professions
statement: Employment history indicates rehabilitation prospects. Members of professions associated with government and the justice system are expected to act with the highest honesty and integrity; failure to do so may aggravate and emphasise just punishment and general deterrence.

refs.q: The employment history of an offender is relevant during sentencing as it is an indication of their prospects for rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.2 – Employment

refs.q: There are also professions associated with government and the justice system whose members are expected to act with highest levels of honesty and integrity, and their failure to do so may be taken as an aggravating factor and emphasise the need for just punishment and general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.2 – Employment

title: Remorse (repentance, contrition)
statement: Remorse is relevant at common law and implicitly under the Act (forfeiture effects and conduct at trial as indicators). Genuine remorse is extremely rare and very important: it enhances rehabilitation prospects and reduces specific deterrence and community protection. A plea made appreciating wrongfulness and impact and wishing to make amends calls for a significant reduction beyond the utilitarian discount. Even genuine remorse does not displace the need to reflect gravity. Genuine remorse differs from feigned remorse, self-pity, depression or anguish at being caught; determination to change and make amends is the indicator. It must be proved on the balance of probabilities on proper evidence (the offender’s own testimony is the most compelling; words and deeds over time are more informative); be cautious before treating a plea as showing more than utilitarian value; long delay before the plea may detract. A victim impact statement cannot disprove remorse. (Footnote 1334’s “Ibid” is resolved to BarbaroVIC by its pinpoint: flag.fn1334_ibid_after_see_also.)

refs.q: Remorse is also referred to as ‘repentance’ or ‘contrition’ and is a relevant consideration at common law and a statutory consideration when sentencing for Commonwealth offences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: It is not directly identified as a relevant consideration under the Victorian regime, but the Act implicitly incorporates it as one by stating that a court may consider the effects of a forfeiture order or an offender’s conduct during trial or hearing as an indicator of remorse.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Genuine remorse is extremely rare and a very important element of sentencing as it enhances the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation and reduces the need for specific deterrence and community protection.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: An offender’s guilty plea made appreciating the wrongfulness of their conduct, its impact on the victim, and wishing to repair any harm out of a wish to clear their conscience also calls for an exercise of mercy in the form of a significant sentence reduction beyond that given to all guilty pleas for their utilitarian value.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: However, even genuine remorse cannot make up for some harms and it does not displace the need for the gravity of offending to be reflected in the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Genuine remorse must be contrasted with feigned remorse, self-pity, or depression. The ‘anguish’ at being caught and punished is not an indication of remorse. An offender’s determination to change their behaviour and to make amends to the extent possible is.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: An offender who wants to rely on remorse in mitigation must ‘satisfy the court there is genuine penitence and contrition and a desire to atone’. This must be established on proper evidence and a court should be cautious before accepting that an offender’s guilty plea indicates remorse warranting more than a utilitarian discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: A court is also entitled to consider a lengthy period of delay between the offending and the guilty plea as detracting from the quality of the offender’s remorse and prospects for rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: The degree of an offender’s true remorse is a question of fact to be determined on the balance of probabilities.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: The most ‘compelling evidence’ of remorse is the offender’s testimony and a court is not bound to accept other ‘second-hand evidence’. The words and deeds of the offender over time are ‘more informative and precise’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Hardship to the offender and the willingness to assume significant burdens to make restitution is a strong indication of remorse.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: A victim impact statement cannot be used to disprove a claim of remorse. The prosecution will ordinarily need to lead admissible evidence in order to disprove a claim of remorse.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: The genuineness of remorse and the time and manner it manifests should be evaluated in light of the overall facts. Timing is relevant in that remorse is generally given less weight the later it appears. But an offender’s remorse is not measured at the time of the offending.

title: Absence of remorse is not aggravating
statement: Absence of remorse cannot aggravate, but may indicate a need for specific deterrence; if it reveals contempt for the victim or the law it may be relevant to culpability and rehabilitation prospects, depending on the case.

refs.q: The absence of remorse cannot be a circumstance of aggravation. But it may indicate a need for specific deterrence. If evidence establishing a lack of remorse reveals a contemptuous attitude to the victim or the law, it may also be relevant to the offender’s moral culpability and prospects for rehabilitation. Whether this is so will depend on the circumstances of the individual case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

title: Doran discount: admissions to conduct otherwise difficult to prove
statement: Admissions to conduct otherwise difficult to prove, or that supply evidence needed for conviction, warrant a “demonstrable discount” to encourage others (the Doran discount), including admissions leading to more or more serious charges. Not confined to unknown crimes or incapable complainants; may apply to a confession after being confronted with evidence if it affected the form of the charge. Depending on the admissions, 30% to 50% may be appropriate — generally more for confession to an unknown crime, less where it adds detail to existing allegations; leniency is called for where proof depends entirely on the confession. A matter of degree and fact.

refs.q: It may be demonstrated by making admissions to conduct that would otherwise have been difficult to prove or that provide the prosecution with evidence necessary to obtain a conviction, and when such a confession is made it warrants a ‘demonstrable discount’ in sentence in order to encourage similar admissions from other offenders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: This significantly mitigating factor is known in Victoria as the ‘Doran Discount’, and it has been held to apply further to admissions that lead to the laying of an increased number of charges or to more serious charges.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: The discount is not confined to cases where the crime was unknown before the confession or where the complainant did not have capacity to give evidence. The discount may also be available where the offender made the confession after the offender was presented with the evidence against them, if that affected the form of the charge.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Depending on the admissions, a discount of 30% to 50% may be appropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: The discount will generally be more substantial when the confession is made to an unknown crime and less when it only provides detail of existing allegations. Nonetheless, if proof depends entirely on the confession, leniency is called for. The amount is a matter of degree and fact depending on the circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

title: Restitution and reparation
statement: Restitution is a common law factor allowing a reduced sentence or shorter non-parole period, but even full reparation does not avoid all punishment. It is always relevant and mitigating and should be encouraged (reparation, remorse, no profit); hardship and willingness to assume burdens get great weight; mitigation is not removed but may be lessened when made by third parties or court order (compare 5.2.8.2 on loss recouped from an insurer: flag.third_party_restitution_weight); an offender must not buy, or appear to buy, a lower or suspended sentence; first-time offers on the plea are viewed cautiously; deferral to allow restitution is rare and viewed cautiously; differences in restitution may explain disparity; failure to make restitution is not aggravating.

title: Guilty plea: statutory consideration and why it is rewarded
statement: The Act requires the court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage any plea or intention to plead occurred. A plea saves the State and victims the cost and trauma of a trial, spares witnesses (especially in homicide and sexual cases) the ordeal of giving evidence, and abandons any chance of acquittal; it is publicly rewarded to encourage pleas because of the public good that follows.

refs.q: The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) requires a court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage in the proceedings any plea or intention to plead occurred.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: A guilty plea saves the State and the victims the cost (human and financial), and trauma of a trial.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: For witnesses and their families, particularly those in homicide and sexual offence cases, a guilty plea spares them from the ordeal of having to give evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: When an accused person offers their plea of guilty, they abandon any chance of being acquitted, even undeservedly.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: For these reasons, an accused person’s plea of guilty is publicly rewarded: the purpose being to encourage offenders to plead guilty because of the significant public good that follows when they do.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: The value of an accused’s plea of guilty is recognised both by the common law and statute.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: The courts have consistently acknowledged the public interest in an accused pleading guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: The economic advantage to the community when a person pleads guilty are the saving of judicial, prosecutorial and legal aid resources, witness fees, and the fees paid to (and the inconvenience experienced by) jurors.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: Pleas of guilty assist victims to put their experiences behind them, to receive vindication and support from their family and friends, and possibly to obtain assistance from the community for any injury they may have suffered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: The other benefits of an accused person pleading guilty are relieved congestion in the courts, and improved finalisation rates for criminal cases with a consequent increase in public confidence in the criminal justice system.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

title: Pleas during the COVID-19 pandemic (and its subsiding)
statement: A plea entered during the currency of the pandemic (while courts worked under its adverse effects) carried greater utilitarian benefit and attracts augmented weight: a significant discount that the court need not quantify, applied consistently and not dependent on venue. The Manual notes that as at the end of 2023 the effects had subsided, but fixes no end date.
logic: (app policy, flag.covid_custody_currency) consider the augmentation only for a plea entered within the pandemic period and not for one entered after 2023; reasoning that applies it to a plea entered after 2023 → caution; a plea entered in 2023, or an unknown plea date → caution (the Manual fixes no end date); never an error either way
note: params subsided_as_at_year records an observation (“It has been noted …”), not a cut-off fixed by the Manual: the app uses it only as a soft (caution-level) limit, never as an error-level date. See flag.covid_custody_currency.

refs.q: In particular, while Victorian courts work under the adverse effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, a sentencing court should ‘view a plea of guilty as carrying with it a greater utilitarian benefit than at other times, and in other circumstances, and, concomitantly, as attracting an augmented mitigatory effect on sentence, simply because the plea will benefit the beleaguered administration of justice’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: All other things being equal, a plea entered during the currency of the pandemic is worth greater weight in mitigation than a plea entered at a time when the community and the courts are not affected by the effects of the pandemic. It should attract a significant discount (which the court does not need to quantify) but not one ‘with a malleable weight, dependent on Court venue….’ The discount for having pled during the pandemic must be applied consistently.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: It has been noted, however, that as at the end of 2023 the effects of the pandemic upon the criminal justice system in Victoria have subsided.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

title: Weight of a guilty plea
statement: Every plea must be considered, with weight depending on the circumstances after specific and sound consideration. A plea need not always produce a discount, and the court is not bound by a Crown concession that it should.

refs.q: Every plea of guilty must be considered in sentencing. But the weight to be given it depends upon the circumstances of each case and should be the result of ‘specific and sound’ consideration. A plea does not always need to result in a sentencing discount, nor is the court bound to accept a Crown concession that a guilty plea should reduce the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight

title: Utilitarian value of the plea
statement: In all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value must be acknowledged by a reduction, regardless of remorse (even a self-interested plea has utilitarian value). The strength of the Crown case is irrelevant to utilitarian value, but the length and complexity of the trial avoided is relevant (the benefit might be considered great where an overwhelmingly complex, lengthy circumstantial case is avoided). Contesting other charges does not diminish the utilitarian value of the pleas entered.

refs.q: In all but exceptional cases, the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction in the sentence imposed. This recognises the objective benefit to the community regardless of whether the plea is accompanied by any evidence of remorse or contrition. Even a plea motivated by self-interest has a utilitarian benefit.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: The strength of the Crown case will have no bearing on the assessment of (and reward for) the utilitarian value of a guilty plea because it does not bear upon the objective benefits of the plea. But the length and complexity of any trial that has been rendered unnecessary by the guilty plea is relevant to the assessment of the utilitarian benefit.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: If the Crown must prove an overwhelmingly complex and lengthy circumstantial case, the benefit of a guilty plea might be considered great.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: When an accused pleads guilty to some charges but contests others, this does not diminish the weight to be attached to the utilitarian benefit of the pleas of guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

title: A plea of not guilty is never aggravating
statement: A not guilty plea is never aggravating: an accused cannot be penalised for insisting on trial, and the court may not increase a proper sentence to mark disapproval of putting the Crown to proof or of a time-wasting or scurrilous defence.

refs.q: While a plea of guilty must always be taken into account as a mitigating factor, a plea of not guilty is never an aggravating factor. An accused person cannot be penalised for insisting on their right to trial, and a court may not mark its disapproval of the accused having put the issues to proof or having presented a time wasting or even scurrilous defence by increasing what is a proper sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: But the principles, however competitive, are entrenched and operate to restrain a wrongful approach to sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

title: The plea as an indicator of remorse; strength of the Crown case
statement: A plea showing genuine remorse, entered at the earliest practical opportunity and saving a trial and witness trauma normally deserves a substantial discount. The strength of the Crown case may bear on whether the plea reflects remorse (a strong case may mean recognition of the inevitable), but care is needed because an offender may be genuinely remorseful whatever the strength; a plea to a weak case generally warrants an additional discount (this additional discount goes to remorse and willingness to facilitate justice, not utilitarian value, on which the strength of the case has no bearing: 7.1.2.1). Where remorse is inferred from the plea, the court should identify its weight and how it was taken into account.

refs.q: A guilty plea that demonstrates genuine remorse, that is entered at the earliest practical opportunity, that saves the State a trial and witnesses both trauma and inconvenience normally deserves a substantial sentencing discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.2 – Indicator of remorse

refs.q: The strength of the Crown case may be relevant when determining the degree to which a guilty plea reflects the offender’s remorse. A strong Crown case may warrant a conclusion that the plea is merely the offender ‘recognising the inevitable’ and a finding that remorse, contrition and willingness to facilitate the course of justice are not indicated. However, care should be taken before concluding that a plea of guilty to a strong Crown case indicates an absence of contrition because whatever the strength of the Crown case an offender may be genuinely remorseful and accepting of responsibility. For guilty pleas where the Crown case is weak, an additional level of discount is generally warranted.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.2 – Indicator of remorse

refs.q: Where remorse may be inferred from a guilty plea, a court should identify the weight it has attributed to the plea and how it was taken into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.2 – Indicator of remorse

title: Timing of the plea (early, late, and pleas that are not late)
statement: An early, unconditional plea ordinarily attracts a substantial discount (normally high if it also evidences remorse and rehabilitation; usually still significant if it only saves costs). A late plea attracts a lower discount. Timing is characterised by when it was first reasonably open to plead guilty. Pleas that are not late are listed below. Where a statutory alternative was available earlier, a later plea is not necessarily “early”. Where a plea is late and the accused caused lengthy, expensive extradition proceedings, the discount may be small. Where the conviction reflects a rejected plea offer, the offender gets the discount that acceptance would have attracted.

not_late.text: plea to a lesser offence shortly after the more serious charge is discontinued

refs.q: when it is made to a lesser offence shortly after the prosecution discontinues a more serious charge;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

not_late.text: plea after other charges are withdrawn, where withholding it reasonably avoided forensic prejudice — but delay whose object or effect is to secure a forensic advantage or avoid a forensic disadvantage on other charges is not reasonable; the Manual does not reconcile the two (flag.plea_timing_forensic_prejudice: caution)

refs.q: when it is entered after the prosecution withdraws other charges, where the accused was reasonably avoiding forensic prejudice by withholding the plea until those other charges were withdrawn.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: However, an accused does not act reasonably in delaying a guilty plea if the object or effect of the delay is to secure a forensic advantage or avoid a forensic disadvantage in relation to any other charged offences;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

not_late.text: plea as soon as told it was the only charge

refs.q: if the offender pleaded guilty to the offence of which they were ultimately convicted as soon as they were told that it was the only charge they would face;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

not_late.text: plea as soon as the charge was amended to the proper factual basis

refs.q: where the offender pleads guilty as soon as a charge was amended to reflect the proper factual basis or particulars of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: A plea given early and unconditionally should ordinarily attract a substantial sentencing discount. A plea made at the earliest opportunity that evidences genuine remorse and prospects of rehabilitation, which saves the State a trial and witnesses trauma and inconvenience, normally justifies a high discount. An early plea that does nothing but save the costs of a trial usually still attracts a significant discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: A late plea attracts a discount, but it will generally be of lower value. How the timing of a guilty plea is characterised depends on the facts of the case and involves establishing the time it could first be said it was reasonably open to the offender to plead guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: However, where a statutory alternative is available, a shift in the factual basis of the allegation will not necessarily mean a later plea is recast as ‘early’ if the offender could have pleaded guilty to the alternative allegation at an earlier stage.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: Where a plea is late, and an accused has caused lengthy expensive extradition proceedings, the discount for the plea may be small.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: Where the ultimate conviction reflects a previously rejected plea offer, the offender should be afforded the discount they would have been given had the plea offer been accepted in recognition of the lost utilitarian value of the offer. An unaccepted plea may also demonstrate acceptance of responsibility, remorse and a willingness to facilitate to course of justice.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

title: Applying the plea discount (head sentence, then non-parole period; mandatory minimums)
statement: The discount is applied consistently with the form of sentence and may change that form. For imprisonment it is applied first to the head sentence, then to the non-parole period (possibly with an additional discount there if the plea evidences rehabilitative prospects). Mandatory minimum regimes do not oust common law principles but modify them (little authority). For suspended sentences (where available) the discount applies to the sentence, then to the part served immediately. (The authority for the suspended-sentence rule is fn 1420, “Ibid.” after a Western Australian mandatory-sentencing case: cite it by section and footnote only — flag.ibid_1420_suspended_sentence_attribution.)

refs.q: The discount for a guilty plea needs to be applied consistently with the form of the sentence, but its application may change the form of the sentence itself.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount

refs.q: Where a sentence of imprisonment is imposed, the discount is first applied to the head sentence as the prisoner must, hypothetically, serve every day of that sentence. Next, the discount is applied to the non-parole period. The plea may even incur an additional discount at this stage if it also evidences rehabilitative prospects.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment

refs.q: A mandatory minimum term of imprisonment can create complications for reductions in sentence for mitigatory factors, including pleas of guilty. A minimum sentencing regime does not oust common law sentencing principles but necessarily modifies both.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment

refs.q: When a suspended or partially suspended sentence is available the discount applies first to the sentence itself and then to the extent the sentence is to be served immediately.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.2 – Suspended sentences

title: Pleas to the gravest offending (competing authority); worst murders
statement: Authorities compete: one line gives more weight to a plea the more serious the crime (utilitarian value and sparing victims); more recent authority asks whether the enormity of the criminality means utilitarian benefit must yield to public protection and the rule of law. For the worst murders a plea is generally a necessary condition for fixing a non-parole period, but a plea will not necessarily save a murderer from life imprisonment. (Competing authority: flag.worst_category_plea_competing_authority.)

refs.q: There are competing authorities on the question of whether an offender pleading guilty to an offence in the ‘worst category’ of offending should be entitled to a discount for their plea.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

refs.q: Reasoning in this way, the greater the seriousness of the crime, the greater the weight to be given to a plea of guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

refs.q: However, more recent authority considers whether the enormity of the offenders’ criminality is such that the utilitarian benefit of their guilty plea must yield to greater considerations such as the protection of the public and the maintenance of the rule of law.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

refs.q: It is now generally held that for the worst instances of murder, the entry of a guilty plea is a necessary condition for the fixing of a non-parole period, but it should not be assumed that a plea will save a murderer from life imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

refs.q: Those cases tend to focus on the utilitarian benefit of the plea and the fact that it spares victims (or their families) from the trauma of giving evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

use: output must include the notional (undiscounted) sentence and NPP when a trigger applies and the plea reduced the sentence
title: Section 6AAA: stating the notional sentence but for the plea
statement: When the sentence involves a custodial order, an order to serve imprisonment, a CCO of two years or more, a fine over 10 penalty units or an aggregate fine over 20 penalty units, and the plea produced a less severe sentence, the court must state the notional sentence it would have imposed after trial — for the overall sentence (total effective sentence and single non-parole period; an aggregate sentence is a single sentence), including the notional non-parole period — and record it. Where the offender pleaded to only some charges, the Court of Appeal has suggested the statement concern the total effective sentence (the Manual says the position is unclear: flag.s6aaa_mixed_pleas → caution, not error). Where not required, the court may still state it (7.1.4; 2.4.9 fn 361 says “must”: flag.s6aaa_scope_2_4_9_vs_7_1_4). Always state the notional (undiscounted) figures. The plea may change the form of sentence, so the notional sentence may be of a different (more severe) type. Failure to make the statement likely does not invalidate the sentence (7.1.4.6; s 103) — report it as a missing statutory statement, not an unlawful sentence.
note: “custodial order” (the first trigger) is not defined in the Manual. App policy: imprisonment (including any order to serve a term) is a trigger; for other custodial dispositions (youth justice/residential centre orders, a DATO’s custodial part, CSTO) treat the requirement as uncertain → caution.
logic: if guilty_plea and plea_reduced_sentence and (imprisonment or (cco and cco_years >= 2) or fine_pu > 10 or aggregate_fine_pu > 20): state the notional sentence with its type (s6aaa.notional_type) and its measure (+ the notional NPP if an NPP is fixed); same type: compare by the type’s measure — imprisonment: notional term ≥ actual term and notional NPP ≥ actual NPP, at least one strictly greater (a statutory minimum may hold the NPP at the same figure); CCO: notional months and unpaid-work hours each ≥ actual with at least one strictly greater; both equal → only if the reasoning states which other conditions the plea reduced, otherwise caution (app policy); one greater and the other smaller → caution (app policy); fine or aggregate fine: notional amount (penalty units or dollars) > actual; different type: the notional type must be more severe in principle.sentence_type_ordering (a comparison it does not settle → caution; as audit.s6aaa_statement); other custodial orders (youth detention, CSTO, RTO, DATO custodial part) → caution (note; flag.s6aaa_custodial_order_undefined); mixed pleas → caution only

refs.q: Specifically, section 6AAA of the Act requires a court, when imposing certain forms of sentence, to state the benefit the offender has received because of their guilty plea.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: The court must articulate a ‘notional sentence’ it would have imposed after trial if the offender had not pleaded guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: • a custodial order; or • an order that the offender serve a term of imprisonment; or • a Community Corrections Order for a period of two years or more; or • a fine exceeding 10 penalty units; or • an aggregate fine exceeding 20 penalty units.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: The notional sentence only needs to be stated if the court has imposed a less severe sentence because of the guilty plea. It also only needs to be stated in relation to the overall sentence, not in relation to individual charges. If a total effective sentence is imposed in respect of multiple offences, the periods to be stated are the total effective sentence and single non-parole period, if any.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: Aggregate sentences are to be treated as a single sentence for the purposes of s 6AAA.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: If a non-parole period is imposed, the notional undiscounted non-parole period must also be stated.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: It is unclear what is expected of the s 6AAA statement when the offender has pleaded guilty to some but not all charges. The Court of Appeal has suggested the notional sentence is to be made regarding only the total effective sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: In cases where a s 6AAA statement is not required because of the form of sentence being imposed, a court may still state the notional sentence that would have been imposed but for the offender’s plea of guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: Where the court states a notional sentence, it must record or cause it to be recorded (whether in writing or in another form) in the records of the court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.1 – Obligation to record

title: Section 6AAA: what is quantified and how (no two-tier sentencing)
statement: The court (at least privately) isolates the plea considerations but need not explain the allocation, though where remorse has an important impact it may indicate whether it was treated in the general synthesis or as part of the plea. The notional sentence is a hypothetical post-trial sentence. The preferred Victorian approach is to take each aspect of the plea (utilitarian value, remorse, admissions, offered assistance) together for the reduction, and remorse and contrition keep independent force. Endorsed method: fix the sentence by instinctive synthesis, then estimate how much longer it would have been without the plea (or fix the notional first and subtract); the method is discretionary but must not become two-tier sentencing.

refs.q: Section 6AAA requires the court (at least privately) to isolate considerations flowing from the plea. However, it does not require the court to explain that allocation in the sentencing reasons.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.1 – Obligation to record

refs.q: However, if a factor such as remorse has an important impact on sentence, it may be appropriate to indicate whether it has been treated as part of the general synthesis or as a consequence of the guilty plea.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.1 – Obligation to record

refs.q: The statement of the notional sentence requires the court, as a hypothetical exercise, to ignore the plea of guilty and determine the sentence that would have been imposed after a trial.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing

refs.q: In Victoria, the preference is to take each aspect of the plea together to arrive at the reduction in sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing

refs.q: Once such factors are considered as part of the reduction in sentence for the plea of guilty, that does not exhaust the mitigating effect of factors such as remorse and contrition. They continue to have independent force in the sentencing process.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing

refs.q: • determine the sentence that should be imposed by the instinctive synthesis; and • attempt to identify how much longer the sentence would have been had the offender not pleaded guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.3 – Methodology

refs.q: An alternative approach is to determine the notional sentence first and then determine the actual sentence by subtracting the benefit attributable to the guilty plea and its attendant considerations from that notional sentence. Ultimately the method is not governed by the Act or authority, and it remains a discretionary decision. However, courts should be cautious not to engage in two-tiered sentencing when applying s 6AAA. It is not permissible to take a starting point and then add or subtract periods of time representing aggravating or mitigating circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.3 – Methodology

refs.q: On this approach, an offender who had made admissions, pleaded guilty, was remorseful and offered to assist authorities would have the combination of these considerations quantified for the purposes of the reduction in their sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing

refs.q: Sometimes, mitigating factors will continue to have force even after they are considered as part of the mitigation for the plea of guilty.

title: Section 6AAA: cooperation undertakings and hypothetical difficulties
statement: Past cooperation is taken into account in the notional sentence; different approaches have been taken for undertakings of future cooperation (unresolved in the Manual: flag.s6aaa_future_cooperation_approaches). Where cooperation and plea are dealt with compendiously, resentencing for failure to cooperate should not increase the sentence by more than part of the discount. The hypothetical is artificial (e.g. sentencing facts may not match a hypothetical trial). Where both s 6AAA and the Commonwealth s 16AC apply, it is not desirable to aggregate the discounts: the processes are better kept separate — the judge assesses what they would have done without the undertaking (the s 16AC specification) and separately identifies the sentence but for the plea. The Court did not say whether the s 16AC specification assumes a plea of guilty or not guilty; the Manual says the disapproval of the aggregate practice suggests the judge should assume a plea of not guilty (Commonwealth; outside the app’s Victorian scope).

refs.q: Past cooperation should be taken into account when declaring a notional sentence, but different approaches have been taken where an offender has given undertakings as to future cooperation.

title: Section 6AAA: status of the notional sentence on appeal
statement: The notional sentence is not part of the sentence and errors in it are not in themselves appealable. Section 6AAA states no consequence for failing to specify the discount, and the Act’s general rule that a failure to give reasons or comply with another procedural requirement does not invalidate a sentence likely applies; failure to make the declaration is an irregularity that will rarely, if ever, justify interference where sufficient weight was given to the plea. Percentage discounts are not always a helpful test of weight. Rarely, the notional sentence may be a particular of manifest excess/inadequacy or insufficient weight to the plea.

refs.q: The notional sentence is not a part of the sentence imposed, and errors or inadequacies in that figure are, in themselves, not appealable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.6 – Appellate issues

refs.q: Moreover, the Court of Appeal has noted that a failure to make the s 6AAA declaration is an irregularity and will ‘rarely, if ever, justify interfering with the sentence’ when sufficient weight has nonetheless been given to the plea of guilty.

refs.q: Accordingly, it is not always helpful to simply consider any percentage discount given to determine whether sufficient weight was given to the guilty plea.

title: Sentence indications (Criminal Procedure Act 2009)
statement: Sentence indications help accused decide early whether to plead guilty. Magistrates’ Court: on its own initiative, once summary jurisdiction is invoked, the magistrate may indicate imprisonment to be served immediately or a sentence of a specified type (type only, not quantum); must not impose a more severe type; another magistrate hears the matter if no plea at the first opportunity (unless parties agree); the application cannot be evidence against the accused. Higher courts: after the indictment is filed, only on the accused’s application with prosecution consent (informal indications are discouraged); a specified type or a specified maximum total effective sentence; no more severe sentence may be imposed. An indication binds only the judicial officer who gave it. Discretion to give one is final (judicial review only); the court may decline for insufficient information on the effect on any victim. A plea after an indication is not necessarily inconsistent with remorse (a question of fact; in NSW such a plea has been given less weight than a plea expressing remorse). For an applicant already in custody, an indication of immediate imprisonment means actual imprisonment from sentence. The binding effect is hard-checked by audit.sentence_indication (intake records the indication and whether the plea was entered on it).

refs.q: The sentence indication schemes in the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) (‘CPA’) are designed to put defendants who may ultimately plead guilty in a position to make this decision early in the proceedings.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication

refs.q: A magistrate may give a sentence indication on their own initiative at any time during a proceeding for a summary offence or an indictable offence that may be heard and determined summarily.

title: Cooperation with authorities: policy and statutory announcement (s 5(2AB))
statement: Encouraging offenders to inform on co-offenders is very much in the public interest. Assistance is considered in mitigation and can produce sentences much lower than otherwise expected — a price society must pay. The discount varies with the level of cooperation, its subjective significance and its actual or potential utility. Section 5(2AB) requires the court to announce that it is imposing a less severe sentence and to have the undertaking and its details noted in the record.

refs.q: It is very much in the public interest that those who commit offences received every encouragement by the courts to inform upon their co-offenders; the courts have long recognised the community interest in fostering ‘dishonour among thieves’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.1 – Policy

refs.q: An offender who assists the authorities is entitled to have that assistance considered in mitigation of sentence. An aspect of this factor in mitigation is its public nature. Section 5(2AB) of the Act requires the court to announce it is imposing a less severe sentence and have the undertaking and its details noted in the record of the court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.1 – Policy

refs.q: The courts’ role in fostering cooperation with authorities is capable of producing sentences much lower than those that would otherwise be expected. This is a price that society must be willing to pay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.1 – Policy

refs.q: The discount varies according to the level of cooperation, its subjective significance, and the utility or potential utility of the assistance given.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.1 – Policy

note: params true_informer_pct_range describes outcomes at the highest level of cooperation (“could attract”): never bounds, a default or a computation. The Manual says courts “sometimes” express discounts as percentages “of the starting point”; do not compute the sentence from a starting point and a percentage (2.1: quantifying a discount is inconsistent with the instinctive synthesis; audit.instinctive_synthesis_not_two_tier). Citing the Court of Appeal’s range descriptively is not two-tier sentencing.
title: Levels of cooperation and the size of the discount (no tariff)
statement: The discount rises or falls with objective and subjective factors: lowest — admissions and a plea; higher — implicating co-offenders, providing information and giving evidence; highest — “true informers” who proactively assist, often undercover and at great risk. Labels matter less than the nature of the assistance and its consequences for the offender. There is no mathematical process, tariff or standard discount; factors include the nature and extent of cooperation, willingness to testify against co-offenders and danger. The Court of Appeal has said the highest level could attract 50% to 66% for a true informer, but each discount must be assessed in context, not mathematically.

refs.q: The discount to be applied will rise or fall according to both objective and subjective factors. The lowest level of cooperation is making admissions and entering a plea of guilty. At higher levels, cooperation may involve implicating co-offenders or providing other information of assistance to authorities and giving evidence in criminal proceedings. The highest-level discount is reserved for so-called ‘true informers’, who assist authorities proactively, acting as ‘undercover’ agents to provide information and evidence, commonly at greatly increased personal risk.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount

refs.q: But terminology is of little assistance: the focus should be on the nature of the assistance that an offender provides and the consequences for the offender of providing that assistance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount

refs.q: Many factors are relevant to the exercise of the discretion in these circumstances and there is no mathematical or mechanical process for fixing the value of the cooperation discount. The discount is determined according to a range of factors, including — but not limited to — the nature and extent of the cooperation, any willingness to give evidence against co-offenders, and any danger flowing from the cooperation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.1 – No ‘standard’ discount

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has said that the highest level of co-operation could attract discounts of 50% to 66% for a ‘true informer’. However there is no ‘tariff’ or standard discount. And the Court has emphasised the need to assess each discount for cooperation in context and to avoid approaching the task in a mathematical way.

title: Assessing the value of cooperation
statement: Assistance is rewarded regardless of motive, though willingness matters (sometimes only voluntary cooperation counts; genuine remorse warrants more). No discount if the offender tailors information to what they know police already have, but not lost if they did not know, if the information proves ineffective, or if authorities do not act on it. The discount is rarely substantial without full disclosure; what matters is the potential to assist as comprehended by the offender. False information earns nothing. Not lost if the person informed on pleads guilty or is acquitted for unrelated reasons. The court does not assess whether the offender will comply with the undertaking.

refs.q: An appropriate reward should be provided for the giving of assistance, regardless of the motivation. But the extent of the discount may depend on the willingness of the disclosure. In some instances, it will only be relevant if the cooperation was voluntary. In others, where the motive is one of genuine remorse and contrition, this will warrant greater leniency.

refs.q: If the offender tailors their assistance to reveal only information they know the authorities already have, there will be no applicable discount. But an offender will not lose the discount if they did not know the authorities already have the information. The reward should be granted if the offender has genuinely cooperated, regardless of whether the information objectively turns out to be effective.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.2 – Identifying the level and value of cooperation

refs.q: Nor will the offender lose the discount if the authorities do not act on the information because, for example, they received it from another source.

refs.q: The full and frank co-operation of the offender is to be encouraged. The discount will rarely be substantial unless the offender discloses everything they know.

refs.q: Indications of valuable assistance may include whether:
