refs.q: Examples of different forms cooperation are:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.4 – Forms of cooperation

refs.q: To this extent the inquiry is into the subjective nature of the offender’s cooperation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.2 – Identifying the level and value of cooperation

title: Assistance on other offences or in other jurisdictions (no double counting)
statement: Assistance on other offences may be considered (but earlier informing gives no immunity for later offending); assistance to interstate or international agencies may be reflected, but must not be double counted — if already rewarded elsewhere the discount is exhausted.

refs.q: Assistance given to authorities may be considered despite being given in relation to offences other than those for which the offender stands to be sentenced, but this does not mean informers accrue some kind of immunity when they offend after giving assistance to authorities earlier.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.6 – Other cooperation

refs.q: And it is not necessary that the assistance be provided in the jurisdiction where the offender is being sentenced. Courts can set a reduced sentence to reflect assistance given to interstate or international law enforcement agencies. However, the sentencing court must ensure that it does not double count the offender’s assistance. Where the offender has already received the benefit of the assistance in another jurisdiction, the sentencing discount will be exhausted.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.6 – Other cooperation

title: Risk of reprisal; victims who give evidence
statement: Exposure to retributive violence is a significant component of the discount; it cannot be calibrated precisely but is generally found substantial; whether the cooperation is known or likely to become known may affect the quantum. A victim who gives evidence as a victim earns no discount for separate offending, unless that assistance causes them to serve imprisonment in protective custody. Protective custody because of cooperation also attracts greater leniency as a hardship (hardship.protection_prisoner); the Manual does not address the overlap — (app policy) do not count the same risk or burden twice, and say how each was weighed.

refs.q: Cooperating with authorities will often expose an offender to a risk of retributive violence. This risk is a significant component of the discount warranted for cooperation with authorities.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

refs.q: It is neither necessary nor possible to calibrate with precision the degree of risk to which a person exposes themselves by giving evidence against co-offenders, though a court will generally find that the risk is substantial.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

refs.q: Because of that difference a sentencing court is entitled to treat the question of whether the cooperation is known, or likely to become known, or not as factor relevant to determining the quantum of the discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

refs.q: There is no policy justification for the victim of an offence to receive a discounted sentence for entirely separate offending, merely because they performed their public duty and give evidence as a victim. However, where assistance by an offender who is also a victim of separate offending causes the offender/victim to serve their imprisonment in protective custody, a reduction in sentence is appropriate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

refs.q: Not every assistance to authority will earn an offender the ‘informer’s discount’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

title: Cooperation must be proved (not asserted from the Bar table)
statement: Assistance must appear from or be proved in evidence; Bar-table assertions are not enough even with Crown consent. The offender must establish on the balance of probabilities that assistance was given and its nature and value.

refs.q: An offender’s assistance should appear from or be proved in evidence to allow a court to assess the appropriate amount of any discount. It is not enough to make assertions from the Bar table, even with the consent of the Crown. It is necessary that the applicant establish, in the course of the plea, on the balance of probabilities, that assistance has been given to the authorities, and the nature and value of that assistance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.8 – Evidentiary matters

title: Combined plea and cooperation discounts must not produce an inadequate sentence
statement: The court may need to revise its initial view of the discount so the combined effect of the plea and promised cooperation does not produce an inadequate sentence; there is no strict rule on sequential or global application.

refs.q: A court will sometimes need to revise its initial views about the discount so that the combined effect of a guilty plea and the promise of future cooperation does not result in an inadequate sentence. While there is no strict rule regarding whether sentencing discounts for a guilty plea and promised cooperation must be applied sequentially or globally, courts have warned against the risk of reducing a sentence unjustifiably due to the combined effect of those two factors.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.9 – Ultimate sentence must still be proportionate to the offending

use: output must announce a reduction for an undertaking to assist and note it for the record; the undiscounted figure is not required (and is undesirable except in the simplest cases)
title: Victorian scheme: announce the reduction for an undertaking to assist; record it
statement: If a less severe sentence is imposed because the offender undertook to assist, the court must announce this and have the undertaking details recorded; non-compliance does not automatically vitiate the sentence but compliance is important. Whether the announcement also extends to past cooperation is unclear in the Manual (7.3.3.1 speaks of an undertaking; 2.4.9 and 7.3.1 of cooperation generally): announce whenever cooperation (past or promised) produced a less severe sentence; error only where an undertaking-based reduction is not announced (flag.s5_2AB_past_vs_future_cooperation; hard-checked by audit.cooperation_statement). The sentence that would otherwise have been imposed need not be stated, and stating it is undesirable except in the simplest cases.

cautions.text: Commonwealth scheme differs (statement only for future cooperation; s 16AC specification) — outside this app’s Victorian scope.

refs.q: But under the Commonwealth scheme this requirement to state that a discount has been given only applies to discounts for future, not past, cooperation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.1 – Identification of discount

cautions.text: Reasons (a suggestion, not a statutory requirement): the Court of Appeal has suggested two versions of remarks — a restricted full version for the parties and a public version silent or veiled on cooperation; published reasons may need to omit or veil the cooperation.

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has suggested that when sentencing an offender who seeks a discount on the plea for cooperating with the authorities, a court should prepare two versions of sentencing remarks:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: • one that fully explains how the offender’s cooperation informed its exercise of the sentencing discretion; and • a second version, which may identify the offender by a pseudonym, that is either silent regarding the cooperation or makes only a ‘veiled reference’ to it.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: The first version is restricted and is published only to the parties, the second is made publicly available.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: Under the Victorian scheme, if a sentencing court imposes a less severe sentence than it otherwise would have because the offender has undertaken to assist law enforcement authorities, the court must both announce that it is doing this and have the details of the undertaking placed in the record. Failure to comply with these requirements does not automatically vitiate a sentencing exercise, but compliance with them remains important.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.1 – Identification of discount

refs.q: However, the quantum of the sentence that the court would have imposed except for the undertaking does not have to be stated. The court may state the sentence that would have been imposed, but it is undesirable to do so except in the simplest cases that have a small number of relevant considerations.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.1 – Identification of discount

refs.q: • one that fully explains how the offender’s cooperation informed its exercise of the sentencing discretion; and • a second version, which may identify the offender by a pseudonym, that is either silent regarding the cooperation or makes only a ‘veiled reference’ to it.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: The first version is restricted and is published only to the parties, the second is made publicly available.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: The fact that a less severe sentence is being imposed because of an offender’s cooperation with investigating and/or prosecuting authorities. The facts and details of the undertaking must be noted in the record of the court.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.9 – Reasons for sentence

refs.q: By proceeding this way, the courts will strike a balance between informing the offender (and any reviewing court) of the reasons for sentence while protecting the offender on the one hand, and by promoting transparency, encouraging other offenders to cooperate and furthering the general deterrent purpose of sentencing on the other.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

title: Failure to fulfil an undertaking: Crown appeal and resentencing
statement: Failure to fulfil an undertaking that produced a benefit can ground a Crown appeal; in Victoria the appellate court may impose the sentence it considers appropriate. Resentencing does not punish the failure but imposes the sentence that would have been imposed without the offer to cooperate (and may restore the original value of other considerations that were reduced).

refs.q: Under both the Victorian and Commonwealth schemes a failure to comply with an undertaking to assist the authorities, which has led to a sentencing benefit, can provide a basis for a Crown appeal to reverse the benefit. In Victoria, the appellate court is empowered to impose the sentence it considers appropriate, having regard to the failure of the respondent to fulfil their undertaking.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.2 – Appeals when there is failure to comply with an undertaking to cooperate

refs.q: The purpose of re-sentencing is not to punish for failing to fulfil the undertaking, but to impose the sentence that would have been imposed if the offender had not offered to cooperate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.2 – Appeals when there is failure to comply with an undertaking to cooperate

refs.q: Where this takes place and an offender subsequently fails to fulfil an undertaking to cooperate, the appellate court may restore the original value of other sentencing considerations, to impose the sentence that should have been imposed if the offender had not given an undertaking to assist.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.2 – Appeals when there is failure to comply with an undertaking to cooperate

use: auditor: flags reliance on prevalence without a disclosed source / opportunity to be heard
title: Prevalence (a circumstance of other offences)
statement: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor of the offender. It need not be proved beyond reasonable doubt, but the court should be sure of it before weighting the synthesis toward general deterrence and giving less weight to mitigation; even then an increase is not inevitable. The court may use general knowledge, but special knowledge must be disclosed with an opportunity to address it; the better view is that any reliance requires procedural fairness and disclosure of the source. Prevalence principles are engaged only if it is used to aggravate. Recent cases focus on the content of the offending (examples below) rather than locality or ethnic community (an exception: more current references to young people committing high volumes of violent crimes, fn 1561). It operates alongside seriousness to increase the importance of general deterrence. The Manual says the material or evidentiary foundation sufficient for a finding of prevalence remains unresolved (evidence or official statistics may be tendered; earlier cases treated some offences as so notoriously prevalent that no proof or prior canvassing was needed): flag.prevalence_evidentiary_foundation. (app policy) Do not aggravate for prevalence without a disclosed source and an opportunity to be heard. The standard is that the court be “sure” (not proof beyond reasonable doubt). The authority for “a circumstance of other offences” (fn 1551, “Ibid.”) is cited by section and footnote only (flag.ibid_1551_prevalence_attribution).

examples.text: family violence; ice; armed robbery; drug importation; child sex tourism; cannabis cultivation; child sexual abuse; firearms

refs.q: • family violence; • ice related offending; • armed robbery; • drug importation; • child sex tourism; • cultivation of cannabis; • sexual abuse of children; and • firearms charges.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.2 – Nature of prevalence

refs.q: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor a circumstance of the offender; but rather is ‘a circumstance of other offences’. When and how prevalence can be invoked as a sentencing consideration has to be navigated carefully.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence

refs.q: Prevalence is not ‘a sentencing fact’ in the Storey sense and so does not need to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. All that is required is that a court should be sure that an offence is prevalent before weighting the instinctive synthesis in favour of general deterrence and giving less weight to mitigatory factors. But even if the court is certain that an offence is prevalent or locally prevalent, an increased sentence is not inevitable. There may be countervailing factors of greater significance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: A sentencing court is entitled to use its general knowledge of the prevalence of particular offences, but when a court relies upon its own knowledge gleaned from some particular area of expertise or experience, it should advise the parties of its intention to use that special knowledge. And an offender (or their counsel) should then be afforded the opportunity to address prevalence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: However, the better view is now that any reliance on prevalence as a sentencing factor demands the court afford the parties procedural fairness on the issue and disclose the source of the reasoning.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: While a judge may observe that an offence is common, or even prevalent, the principles applicable to ‘prevalence’ will not be invoked unless the court uses that consideration to aggravate the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: In the past, courts have sometimes found prevalence relevant to a particular locality or ethnic community. However, more recent cases focus on the content of the offending itself.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.2 – Nature of prevalence

refs.q: The prevalence of a crime is a factor that operates independently alongside the seriousness of the offence to place increased importance on the sentencing purpose of general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.2 – Nature of prevalence

refs.q: There remain unresolved issues as to the material or evidentiary foundations sufficient for a finding of prevalence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: Evidence may be adduced, or official statistics tendered to establish prevalence.
There are earlier cases that state the prevalence of some offences is so notorious that no proof, and no prior canvassing of the issue is required.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: An exception is in more current references to Young people committing high volumes of violent crimes.
Not every sentencing consideration is derived from the offender or the offending: some considerations have their sources in policy.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations

refs.q: Sentencing judges often make observations on the incidence in the community of a particular offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: Ideally, this will be discernible from the sentencing reasons, but it may also be seen in the discussion upon the plea, or by an examination of the sentence imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

title: Delay: the unfairness limb and the rehabilitation limb
statement: Significant delay (interview to charge; charge to trial) can be a powerful mitigating factor, but there is no automatic discount; undue prosecution delay makes a discount much more likely. Two limbs: unfairness (anxiety of a charge hanging over the offender — not eliminated by failure to confess undisclosed offences) and rehabilitation (progress during the delay and good prospects). Their operation depends on cause, length and consequences, with understanding and flexibility. Some evidence is required for either limb (a psychological report may support anxiety, though anxiety may sometimes be accepted without it); full weight on the rehabilitation limb requires both remorse and rehabilitation — mere non-offending is relevant but not in itself sufficient (it attracts less than full weight). Delay affects both head sentence and non-parole period (not as an application of totality). Reasons should refer to delay, and mentioning only one limb may suggest the other was ignored.

refs.q: Significant delay between the time an offender is interviewed by police and the time charges are laid, as well as delay between the laying of charges and trial, can be a powerful mitigating factor. However, delay in itself creates no automatic right to a sentencing discount. The most that can be said is that where the prosecution unduly delays bringing the matter to court there is much more likely to be a discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: There are two limbs to delay as a mitigating factor. The first concerns unfairness to the offender in that a charge (or its prospect) was ‘hanging over’ their head and caused them anxiety (‘unfairness limb’). These effects are not eliminated by the offender’s failure to confess to undisclosed offences during the period of delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: The second limb concerns whether during the period of the delay the offender made progress towards rehabilitation and if prospects of ongoing rehabilitation are good (‘rehabilitation limb’).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: How these two limbs operate to mitigate sentence depends upon the cause of the delay, the length of the delay and the consequences of the delay. The presence of delay calls for ‘a considerable measure of understanding and flexibility in approach’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: Where delay is relevant to sentence, it is prudent for the court to refer to that factor in its sentencing remarks. Further, while a court does not need to refer to each limb of delay separately, where it specifically refers to one limb and not to the other, this may call into question whether the limb not mentioned has been accorded any weight in the sentencing synthesis.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: Where an offender relies on either limb of delay, they must provide some evidence to support the submission.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

refs.q: Where the unfairness limb is invoked, a psychological report may support distress endured by the offender. But there may also be cases where depending on the duration of the delay, its cause, and other circumstances, a court might accept that the delay caused anxiety to the offender without the need for supporting evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

refs.q: Evidence of the rehabilitation limb will need to address its twin aspects: remorse and rehabilitation. Both must be demonstrated for the court to give full weight to this limb. The abstinence from further offending will be relevant but not, in itself, sufficient. Evidence that an offender has made significant positive changes in their life enables the court to mitigate for this aspect of delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

refs.q: Where delay is a relevant sentencing factor, it will be relevant to both head sentence and non-parole period. It is not an application of the totality principle for a sentence to be reduced because of the strain that an offender experiences by having a matter hanging over their head.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.5 – Form of impact on mitigation

title: Delay: when it is “undue” and who is responsible
statement: Delay need not be inordinate; if unduly long it may and often will mitigate. Whether undue depends on elapsed time, the nature/complexity/sophistication of the offence, the investigation required, the period of a series of offences and the offender’s cooperation or obstruction — a matter of degree and common sense. In sexual abuse cases delay in detection or complaint is common and often cannot be relied on. Delay mitigates most where the offender is not responsible: contesting charges is never the offender’s fault, but a late plea after asserting a trial against an overwhelming case cannot be used to claim delay; delay attributable to the offender (absconding, non-cooperation, inaction) gets less significance (an absconder’s rehabilitation may still be reflected in a shorter non-parole period). Witness fear of the accused may make delay not undue (the court may still take rehabilitation into account). Plea negotiations do not necessarily disentitle the offender unless used as a deliberate delaying tactic (such cases are likely rare; but see Ververis, fn 1599); challenging the validity of legislation does not reduce it. Delay caused by prosecution or system is more likely to be major (authorities must act promptly); where delay is relied on as unfairness rather than as harm to the offender, prosecution or investigator responsibility assumes greater significance. Where offending over a long period required long and complex investigations, the weight of delay may be reduced (fn 1586). Trial length generally does not mitigate unless extraordinary. Lack of explanation does not of itself justify a greater reduction.

refs.q: A delay does not need to be inordinate before it may be considered in mitigation. But if it is ‘unduly long’ it may and often will be taken as a mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: • its elapsed time; • the nature, complexity and sophistication of the offence; • the extent of the investigation needed to prepare for a charge and proof of the offence; • for a series of offences, the period of time over which they were committed; and • the degree to which the offender or suspect cooperated with authorities, or conversely their lack of cooperation or any obstruction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: This is not an exhaustive list. Determining if delay was undue ‘is essentially a matter of degree to which common sense is to be applied’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: Where the crime being prosecuted is sexual abuse, the accused is often not able to rely upon delay in mitigation because delay in the detection or complaint of such abuse is a common consequence of the nature of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: Delay is most commonly a direct mitigating circumstance where the responsibility for that delay does not lie with the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Delay that is solely attributable to the fact that an offender exercises their right to contest criminal charges will never be considered the ‘fault’ of the offender, for the purpose of considering the effect of the delay on them and the extent to which that delay is mitigatory.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: On the other hand, defendants cannot be encouraged to delay sentence by asserting an intention to stand trial in the face of an overwhelming prosecution case, and then at the door of the court pleading guilty and asserting the delay as relevant to mitigation of their sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Where delay can be positively attributed to the offender, courts will give less significance to delay, even to the point of giving less credit for rehabilitation established during that period.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: • absconding; • lack of cooperation with investigators; and • standing by while doing nothing to bring the case to fruition.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: However, an absconding offender’s rehabilitation will not necessarily lose all significance. One way to achieve the balance between competing considerations is to reflect the offender’s demonstrated rehabilitation by imposing a shorter non-parole period than would otherwise have been imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Delay may not be ‘undue’ where it is explained by a witness’s fear of the accused. However, while the court may decline to compensate delay in these circumstances, it may still take into account any rehabilitation of the offender between the time of offending and sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: An offender’s decision to enter into plea negotiations will also not necessarily disentitle them from the benefit of a discount for delay, unless they use the negotiations as a deliberate delaying tactic. Such cases are, however, likely to be rare.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Lastly, an offender’s decision to challenge the validity of the legislation under which they are charged cannot reduce the significance of delay as a mitigatory factor.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Delay is more likely to be a major mitigatory factor where the prosecution or the justice system is responsible for delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: When the prosecuting authorities have in fact unduly delayed bringing the matter to court, there is much more likely to be a discount, without the need to have regard to its particular consequences.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: Prosecuting authorities must act promptly when they have evidence of serious criminality.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: Generally, the length of a trial will not be able to be used in mitigation. However, where a trial is of extraordinary duration, it may be appropriate to take this factor into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: But the absence of an explanation for the delay cannot, by itself, justify any greater reduction than if it was satisfactorily explained. In effect explanations for delay are relevant only in so far as they may demonstrate that the offender is responsible for it.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.3 – Unexplained delay

refs.q: But see R v Ververis [2010] VSCA 7, [14].

Where an offender relies on delay as a source of unfairness, rather than as being the product of harm to themselves, then the extent to which the prosecution or investigators are responsible for that delay will assume greater significance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: If the subject offending was committed over such a period, and in such a way that long and complex investigations were necessary, the weight attributable to delay may be reduced.
Whether a delay is ‘undue’ depends on a range of factors, including:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: Some of the ways an offender might contribute to delay are:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: The question of how and if delay might affect a court’s exercise of the sentencing discretion will vary according to the circumstances of the case.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: Sometimes there is no or only insufficient explanation for delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.3 – Unexplained delay

title: Delay: consequences (additional punishment, rehabilitation, change of regime)
statement: Unfairness limb: delay may be additional punishment or unfairness requiring compensation (natural anxiety until arraignment; ordinarily mitigating if unduly long), including a life put “on hold” after an early plea where imprisonment is likely, or strict bail conditions (curfew) during lengthy delay. Rehabilitation limb: full weight requires both remorse and reformation (less for mere non-offending); delay mitigates where there has been a substantial positive change; where rehabilitation is achieved, the focus may move to preserving progress; prospective rehabilitation may authorise a merciful approach and point to a rehabilitative disposition or earlier return to the community; the longer the non-offending, the better the prospects; ageing, onerousness of prison and genuine remorse may also arise. Structural: delay that makes a person who offended as a child liable to the adult regime may mitigate where there is a significant degree of rehabilitation and no further offending; similarly, delay that precludes the youth justice system may mitigate (less weight if a youth sentence would not have been open given gravity).

refs.q: This limb of delay is mitigating because it indicates additional punishment of the offender or carries an unfairness that requires compensation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: There is the natural anxiety occasioned to a person suspected of or charged with an offence until arraignment. If this period is unduly long it may, and ordinarily will, be appropriate to reflect it by way of mitigation of the sentence to be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: Delay where the outcome of the case is likely to be imprisonment, and the offender has put their life ‘on hold’ after an early guilty plea might be an additional punishment that should be considered on sentencing. Similarly, in some circumstances being subjected to strict bail conditions, including curfew, during a lengthy period of delay may be mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: Both aspects of rehabilitation — remorse and reformation — must be demonstrated in order for a court to give full weight to rehabilitation. Less than full weight will be accorded where reliance is placed merely on abstinence from further offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: Delay will thus be mitigating where there has been a substantial and positive change in an offender’s personal circumstances between the time of the offending and the disposition of the matter.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: Where rehabilitation is not just prospective, but achieved, the focus may move from the need to promote rehabilitation, to the need to preserve the progress already achieved.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: The length of any delay will be relevant where an offender has not committed any further offences during the period of the delay. This is because the longer the period of non-offending, the greater are the offender’s rehabilitation prospects.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: • the offender may have aged, making reoffending less likely; • the offender’s age or life expectancy may make a sentence of imprisonment more onerous; and • they may have expressed genuine remorse in the sense of repentance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: The fact that a delay means that an offender is liable to a different statutory regime, as in the case of a child offender subsequently prosecuted as an adult, may be taken into account in mitigation of penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.3 – Structural consequences

refs.q: This mitigation is available when the offender has displayed a significant degree of rehabilitation and there has been no further offending. It recognises the fact that the assessment of the nature and gravity of the crime, and of the offender's moral culpability, must take into account that what was done was done as a child, or as a person of immature years, and not as an adult or a person of greater maturity.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.3 – Structural consequences

refs.q: Similarly, where a delay in prosecution precludes an offender from being dealt with in the youth justice system, which may otherwise have been available had the offender been dealt with more expeditiously, this may mitigate the penalty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.3 – Structural consequences

refs.q: However, the weight given to this fact may be reduced where the offence is of such gravity that service of a sentence in the youth justice system would not have been open on the facts.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.3 – Structural consequences

refs.q: Prospective rehabilitation may warrant mitigation of sentence by authorising a merciful approach and by indicating the imposition of a disposition directed at rehabilitation, or at least, the earlier return of the offender to the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: Other rehabilitative aspects of the changes that may unfold during a period of delay are:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: The two principal direct consequences of delay in this limb are its impact as additional punishment, and as producing unfairness.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: These consequences are often considered as one.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: The sentence is reduced in recognition of the fact that that the sentence has been hanging over the offender for an unreasonable time.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.1 – Unfairness limb

refs.q: Delay provides an opportunity for rehabilitation to proceed before sentencing, thus permitting a court to assess both the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation and any achieved rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: This recognises the community’s vested interest in ensuring the continuation of any process of rehabilitation that has already commenced.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

refs.q: However, as noted, a mere absence of reoffending will mean less than full weight of the delay will be applied in mitigation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

title: Hardship of sanction: three limbs; exceptionality only for hardship to family
statement: Hardship measures the consequence of the sanction on the offender given their circumstances. It may be experienced by (1) the offender personally, (2) the offender’s family or associates, (3) the offender through responsibility for family hardship. Limbs 1 and 3 need no exceptional hardship; limb 2 requires exceptional circumstances (7.6) — but see 7.6.4: for Victorian offences the test now appears to be hardship rising above the general hardship suffered by prisoners’ families and so significant that it will weigh heavily (flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality: where mitigation rests on that formulation with cogent evidence, caution rather than fail). The Act provides for hardship in recording a conviction; other hardship is a common law consideration.

refs.q: This hardship is not a circumstance of the offender but is a measure of the consequence of a sanction on the offender considering their circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: • the offender, through their personal experience of the sanction; • the offender’s family (and sometimes other associates of the offender); and • the offender, through their sense of responsibility for the hardship experienced by their family.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: Limbs one and three do not require the offender to establish any ‘exceptional’ hardship to mitigate sentence. The second limb, hardship to the family (or other associates) of the offender, demands that the offender establish exceptional circumstances before it will go to mitigating sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: In Victoria, the Act provides for consideration of hardship in relation to the imposition of a conviction. The additional hardship of other sanctions for the offender is a relevant consideration at common law, but the general concept has not been recognised in the statute.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.1 – Legal bases of mitigation for hardship of sanction

refs.q: Hardship may be experienced by:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: Courts are frequently urged to mitigate sentence on the basis of matters that make a sanction harder upon the particular offender than on others sentenced for the same offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

title: Protective custody
statement: Protective custody (informers, child sex offenders, former police) is relevant; weight depends on why protection is needed, the circumstances, likely duration and the actual effect (regimes vary from near-solitary to little hardship). Both counsel should provide information on the true conditions. Informers get more leniency than other protection prisoners. A real risk that threats will be carried out requires adjustment, assessed within the instinctive synthesis (not as a departure from an otherwise appropriate sanction). No significance if placement within the system results from the offender’s own past conduct (e.g. violence towards others, drug use, refusing to comply with the ordinary standards needed to keep prison safe). Where protection results from cooperation, see also coop.risk_to_offender (do not count the same risk twice).

refs.q: The main categories of protection prisoners are informers, child sex offenders and former police officers. Where a prisoner is being held in protective custody, that is a factor relevant to sentence. The extent to which it is to be taken in the prisoner's favour depends upon why protection is needed, the particular circumstances, and likely duration of the protection.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: In assessing the weight to be given to this factor, the court must assess the actual effect on the offender of their classification as a protection prisoner. The degree of restriction varies greatly from one case to the other.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: If a submission is made that such a matter is relevant to sentencing, it is incumbent upon counsel for both the prosecution and the defence to provide such information as is available as to the true circumstances of protective custody and the actual hardship protective custody is likely to cause.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: The leniency to be given to a prisoner placed in protection because of cooperation is greater than that allowed other protection prisoners, for example corrupt police officers and sex offenders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Nevertheless, in circumstances where there is a real risk that the threats will be carried out, a court must adjust the sentence accordingly.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Assessment of the risk must factor into the instinctive synthesis. A sentencing judge must not determine an appropriate sanction in the absence of a risk and then consider whether the risk provides a sufficient basis to depart from the otherwise appropriate sanction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: If the offender’s placement within the system is attributable to their own past conduct such as violence towards others, or drug use, or the refusal to comply with the ordinary standards that must be maintained if the prison environment is to remain safe then no significance can be attributed to it when considering the sentence to be imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Some regimes will be very restrictive and involve circumstances very close to the solitary confinement of past days. Others will involve little comparative hardship.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

title: Separation from family (offender’s own anguish)
statement: Anguish at being unable to care for a family member may mitigate if it makes imprisonment more burdensome or materially affects specific deterrence or rehabilitation; weight depends on the circumstances and can never produce a sentence inappropriate to the gravity. Incarceration commonly involves some separation from family, so this hardship is relevant only in limited circumstances. The Corrections Act allows the Secretary to let a parent have a child live with them in prison.

refs.q: An offender’s anguish at being unable to care for a family member may properly be a mitigating factor, if the court is satisfied this will make imprisonment more burdensome or that it materially affects the need for specific deterrence or the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.2 – Separation from family

refs.q: The weight to be attributed to this factor will depend on the circumstances and can never result in a sentence that is otherwise not appropriate for the gravity of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.2 – Separation from family

refs.q: Incarceration will commonly involve some level of separation of the offender from their family, but their hardship is relevant only in limited circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.2 – Separation from family

refs.q: Note also that the Corrections Act 1986 (Vic) gives the Secretary of the Department of Justice the power to allow a parent of a child to have the child live with them in prison.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.2 – Separation from family

refs.q: Hardship to the offender’s family is a discrete consideration, dealt with below.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.2 – Separation from family

title: Hardship of imprisonment from age or ill health
statement: If age directly affects the hardship of imprisonment it may mitigate; deal with old age and ill health separately, as age alone is not mitigating in this sense; an elderly adult may not be a suitable subject for parole. Ill health counts where it directly increases hardship (examples include lung cancer with a short prognosis allowing a non-parole adjustment for immediate release); custodial disruptions for health care and a brain injury have been held insufficient. Mental illness or impairment and poor physical health are among the most significant causes of an increased burden of imprisonment; the main treatment is in 6.2 (factor.physical_health; the Verdins items).

refs.q: This part deals with hardship as it relates to youth and old age.

If age has a direct effect on the hardship of imprisonment, this may operate to mitigate the sentence. Care should be taken to deal with the effects of old age and ill health separately, as age alone is not mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.3 – Age

refs.q: However, the Court of Appeal has said that despite this burden, an elderly adult is not a suitable subject for adult parole and the Parole Board’s activities are better directed at younger offenders who can derive a benefit from supervision.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.3 – Age

refs.q: The following are examples of where the prisoner’s ill health arose as a consideration because of its direct effect on the hardship of imprisonment:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: lung cancer, with prognosis of three to six months’ survival, allowed adjustment of non-parole period to allow for immediate release;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: custodial disruptions for health care did not amount to increased hardship requiring sentencing;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: brain injury not sufficient to reduce sentence for hardship.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: Mental illness or impairment, and poor or impaired physical health are among the most significant circumstances leading to an increased burden of imprisonment.
• a prisoner with cerebral palsy having to spend part of their imprisonment in a unit for intellectually disabled prisoners;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: • failure to comply with medication regime as the result of mental illness made prison more burdensome;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: • diagnosis of terminal cancer and incarceration preventing the appellant from accessing clinical trials found to be burdensome;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: • asbestos exposure and medical evidence suggesting increased risk of developing asbestos-related injury;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

title: Foreign nationals; religion
statement: A foreign national far from family support finds prison more burdensome — always relevant, weight varying with language and cultural differences, the offending and family ties. Ordinarily little weight if the offender came to Australia intending to offend, and it may also be given little weight if they opportunistically offended while visiting for an innocent purpose; a court may give it greater weight for a lawful visitor who offends through gross negligence (e.g. culpable driving); hardship is generally greater for offenders from vastly different countries (isolation). Religious practices likely to make the offender a target may be considered.

refs.q: A foreign national imprisoned in an Australian jail will find prison more burdensome because they will be far from the support of family and friends. This is always relevant to sentence. However, the weight given to this factor will vary from case to case. Factors relevant to that assessment include the extent of any language or cultural differences between Australia and the offender’s country of origin, the circumstances of the offending and the extent of any family ties in the offender’s country of origin.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.5 – Nationality and religion

refs.q: If the offender entered Australia with the intention of committing a crime, the hardship of imprisonment here will ordinarily be given little weight. Similarly, the hardship of a foreign national’s incarceration in Australia may also be given little weight if they entered for an innocent purpose – for example, a holiday – and opportunistically seized the chance to commit an offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.5 – Nationality and religion

refs.q: However, if the offender comes to Australia for a lawful purpose, and commits an offence through gross negligence, such as culpable driving, a court may consider the hardship to be of greater weight.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.5 – Nationality and religion

refs.q: Where the offender is from a country that is vastly different to Australia, the hardship of their incarceration will generally be greater and therefore more mitigating on account of the social or linguistic isolation they are likely to experience. Where an offender’s religious practices are likely to make them a target in prison, this may also be taken into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.5 – Nationality and religion

title: Pregnancy; transgender prisoners
statement: Gender alone is no basis for differential treatment, but pregnancy may make custody more onerous and should be considered (it may not avoid custody or shorten a sentence justice requires). A shorter term may be necessary for a transgender woman at risk and under protection in a men’s prison; prison is generally more onerous for transgender prisoners.

refs.q: Gender alone does not form the basis for differential treatment in sentencing. However, the pregnancy of an offender may make incarceration more onerous and should be considered. But it may not suffice to avoid a custodial term for a woman, nor will a due date necessarily have the effect of shortening a sentence where justice demands a longer sentence be served.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.6 – Gender

refs.q: It may also be necessary to shorten a custodial term for a transgender woman who will have to serve her sentence in a men’s prison where she will be at risk and under protection. In fact, prison in general is more onerous for transgender prisoners and when sentencing a court should take this into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.6 – Gender

title: Prospect of deportation
statement: Likely deportation is relevant if it makes imprisonment more onerous or loses the chance to settle permanently, depending on personal circumstances and actual hardship; limited weight for particularly serious offending; visa cancellation and deportation are not extra-curial punishment. Evidence of both the likely risk and its impact is required, sufficient for sensible quantification; a reduction is appropriate if certain, and may be if probable. Without evidence or a concession the court need not consider it, but mandatory cancellation triggered by the sentence (the Migration Act does so for a sentence of one year or more, subject to revocation) lifts it above speculation. Unusual connections to Australia should be considered. It is error to artificially lower a sentence to avoid the Migration Act. Offence-specific mandatory cancellation (e.g. child sex offences) does not remove deportation as a consideration.

refs.q: The prospect that an offender will be deported following sentence is relevant to sentence if it will make the burden of imprisonment more onerous or may result in the offender losing the opportunity to settle permanently in Australia. But this depends on the personal circumstances of the offender and a court should not consider the possibility of deportation as a mitigatory factor unless it will actually be a hardship for the offender. Moreover, it will be given limited weight in cases where the offending is particularly serious, and neither the cancellation of an offender’s visa nor their consequent deportation will constitute extra-curial punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: There must also be evidence of both the likely risk of deportation and the impact of that risk. Specifically, the evidence must be ‘sufficient to permit a sensible quantification of that risk to be undertaken’. A reduction will be permissible and appropriate where the prospect of deportation (and its impact) is certain. It may also be appropriate where deportation and its adverse impacts are probable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: Without evidence or a prosecution concession, a court need not consider the possibility of deportation. However, when mandatory cancellation of an offender’s visa under the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) is triggered by the sentence imposed, the potential for their deportation is elevated and this lifts that consideration above being a completely speculative possibility.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: Further, where there are unusual circumstances demonstrating a connection to Australia – such as a lengthy period of residency before the commission of the offence, or where the offender’s family have made considerable financial sacrifices to send the offender to Australia – the court should consider these matters.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: As noted, the Migration Act may make visa cancellation mandatory and it does so if an offender is sentenced to one year of imprisonment or more (unless the relevant Minister is satisfied there is a reason to revoke the cancellation). It is, however, error for a sentencing court to artificially lower a sentence in order to avoid the consequences of the Migration Act.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: There are also provisions that make visa cancellation mandatory for specific kinds of offences, including child sex offences. But these provisions do not remove the prospect of deportation as a proper matter for consideration at sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: Although the quantification of the potential for deportation in any case is subject to the evidence or any concession by the prosecution.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

title: Fresh evidence of hardship in custody (appeals)
statement: New evidence may be admitted on appeal if it relates to events since sentence and shows the true significance of facts existing at sentence, but not if it only shows the sentence turned out to be excessive.

refs.q: • relates to events which occurred since the sentence was imposed; and • demonstrates the true significance of facts in existence at the time of the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.3 – Fresh evidence of hardship in custody

refs.q: Fresh evidence is not admissible where it relates only to events that have occurred after sentence and show the sentence has turned out to be excessive.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.3 – Fresh evidence of hardship in custody

refs.q: New evidence may be admitted if it:
