title: Hardship to family or third parties (exceptional circumstances)
statement: Third-party hardship is not normally mitigating, but the court may mitigate if satisfied there are exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal previously described the Victorian test as “highly exceptional” or where mercy is irresistible; it appears now that for Victorian offences the circumstances must rise above the general (sometimes tragic) hardship commonly suffered by prisoners’ families and be so significant they will weigh heavily (flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality). Generally only for especially vulnerable dependants (or several). Requires cogent evidence (possibly a combination of lesser hardships); rare; a question of fact and degree. Not a “passport to freedom”; may affect type and quantum of sentence and ameliorative orders; a reduction must be capable of ameliorating the hardship.

cautions.text: The Manual says: “the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal has said there is no exceptionality requirement for Commonwealth offences and this is now followed by the Victorian Court of Appeal.” Whether that is confined to Commonwealth offences is not stated (Commonwealth sentencing is outside this app’s scope; see the flag).

refs.q: However, the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal has said there is no exceptionality requirement for Commonwealth offences and this is now followed by the Victorian Court of Appeal.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: Hardship to a third party as a consequence of imprisonment is not normally a mitigating circumstance. But a court has discretion to mitigate sentence when that sentence causes hardship to a third-party and it is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: For Victorian offences, the Court of Appeal has previously said that hardship to third parties is only relevant in mitigation where it is ‘highly exceptional’ or ‘the exceptional case where the plea for mercy is seen as irresistible’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: It appears now that for Victorian offences, the circumstances must be such that they rise above the general and sometimes tragic hardship commonly suffered by the families of imprisoned offenders; they must be ‘so significant that they will weigh heavily in the sentencing calculus’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: This consideration will generally only arise where the third party is an especially vulnerable dependent of the offender, or where there are a number of vulnerable dependents.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: Moreover, there must be cogent evidence that the offender’s imprisonment would expose the family member or third party to this hardship. This may also be established by a combination of lesser hardships to multiple family members. These cases will be rare. Whether or not, in any particular case, family hardship is sufficient to be significantly mitigating is a question of fact and degree.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: A finding of such circumstances is also not a ‘passport to freedom’ but simply one factor that can be taken into account. And where family hardship may reduce sentence, it may also be relevant to the type of sentence imposed, the quantum of sentence, and any ameliorative orders that may be made. To attract a reduction in sentence, the reduction would have to be capable of ameliorating the circumstances of the hardship claimed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

title: COVID-19 custodial conditions
statement: The Manual records that courts should be mindful, “in the present time”, that pandemic measures made custody significantly more restrictive, so time in custody has been and is likely to continue to be significantly more punitive than its numerical equivalent. (Elsewhere, in the guilty plea context, the Manual notes that as at the end of 2023 the pandemic’s effects on the Victorian criminal justice system had subsided.)

cautions.text: Check currency: the Manual notes the pandemic’s effects on the criminal justice system had subsided by the end of 2023 (stated in the guilty plea section).

refs.q: It has been noted, however, that as at the end of 2023 the effects of the pandemic upon the criminal justice system in Victoria have subsided.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: It is important, ‘in the present time’, for a court to be mindful of the fact that the conditions of incarceration will be significantly more restrictive and difficult because of the steps taken by prison authorities to prevent the spread of the COVID-19 virus in the prison population.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.5 – COVID-19

refs.q: Any period of time in custody has been and is likely to continue to be ‘significantly more punitive than its numerical equivalent before the onset of the current pandemic’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.5 – COVID-19

title: Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders as punishment (totality)
statement: Totality generally requires account of all punishment, including ancillary punishment, subject to legislative exceptions. Confiscation may be punitive and considered; compensation and restitution orders are not punitive and are not considered. Forfeiture that merely disgorges profit is not considered (the Act); forfeiture going further, or of previously owned property, may be. Proportionality requires the nature and extent of forfeiture to be considered, but it does not require mitigation: consider whether it has a disproportionate or exceptional effect and a substantial deterrent effect. Future forfeiture may be considered with sufficient evidence. The offender bears the onus: evidence enabling a positive finding on the balance of probabilities (direct evidence from the offender plus confirmation of the lawful source of funds; a solicitor relaying assertions is not enough). No account if property is likely to be excluded as lawfully acquired (Confiscation Act s 22). Weight varies with the circumstances.

refs.q: In sentencing, the principle of totality makes it generally appropriate to take account of all punishment formally inflicted upon the offender, even of those in ancillary form. However, there are some specific legislative exceptions.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders

refs.q: Confiscation orders may sometimes be seen as punitive, and so considered in sentencing, because they are ‘part of the retribution exacted from offenders on behalf of the community’. By contrast compensation and restitution orders, which benefit private victims of crime, are not regarded as punitive and are not considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders

refs.q: The Act provides that when a forfeiture order has the effect of disgorging any profit obtained from the offending it is not to be considered in sentencing. This is because there is no punishment in merely restoring the offender to the position they occupied before the offending occurred. However, if the forfeiture order goes further or relates to previously owned property, this may be punitive and be taken into consideration when sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.1 – Forfeiture orders

refs.q: The principle of proportionality requires that the nature and extent of any forfeiture of property be considered in fixing sentence, but forfeiture orders will not require mitigation of the penalty. The court must consider whether forfeiture will have a disproportionate or exceptional effect on the offender and if the order will have a substantial deterrent effect.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.1 – Forfeiture orders

refs.q: It is proper for a court to take future forfeiture into account. However, there does need to be sufficient evidence before the court to enable an assessment to be made of the likely effect of the forfeiture upon the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.2 – Future forfeiture

refs.q: The offender bears the onus of establishing forfeiture as a mitigating circumstance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.3 – Onus of proof

refs.q: Where an offender seeks to rely in mitigation upon the loss of benefits in excess of profits derived from the commission of the offence, the offender must produce evidence to enable the court to make a positive determination on the balance of probabilities. The burden will not be discharged by evidence from the applicant’s solicitor as to the applicant’s assertions about forfeiture. Direct evidence from the applicant, together with confirmatory evidence as to the lawful source of the funds used to acquire the property, is required.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.3 – Onus of proof

refs.q: Where there is likely to be a successful application to have the property excluded pursuant to s 22 of the Confiscation Act 1997 (Vic), because the property can be established as lawfully acquired, there is no reason to take account of forfeiture because the offender will not suffer the additional punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.3 – Onus of proof

refs.q: Where it is determined that a forfeiture or pecuniary penalty order should be considered in sentencing, the question then is what weight it should be given. This will vary with the circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.4 – Weight to be given to forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders

refs.q: Possible future forfeiture presents a particular difficulty for a sentencing court as the court will not be able to measure the extra punishment, if any, that may flow from future forfeiture.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.2 – Future forfeiture

refs.q: For one example of how such loss is treated see R v Gant.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.4 – Weight to be given to forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders

refs.q: In that case, lawfully acquired property to the value of $825,000 was forfeited as it was the building in which fraudulent artworks were said to have been painted.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.4 – Weight to be given to forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders

note: not to be considered for any purpose: the consequence can neither shorten nor lengthen the sentence (audit.collateral_consequences fails both).
title: Consequences under sex offender registration and working with children laws are not considered
statement: The court must not consider any consequence under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004 or the Working With Children Act 2005 arising from the sentence, whether automatic or by court order.

refs.q: A sentencing court is not to consider any consequence that may arise under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004 (Vic) or the Working With Children Act 2005 (Vic) from the imposition of sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.2 – Punishment in registration as sexual offender

refs.q: This applies to all consequences under the Act, regardless of whether the order is made automatically or by court order.

title: Continuing detention orders (Commonwealth terrorism regime)
statement: Commonwealth continuing detention orders (Criminal Code s 105A.3) may require an offender convicted of, generally speaking, terrorism-related offences to be detained after their sentence ends, if they are serving imprisonment and will be at least 18 when it ends, or are under a continuing or interim detention order; an order lasts at most three years, though successive orders may be made, and a court sentencing for a terrorism-related offence must warn the offender that an application may be made (s 105A.23). For sentencing they are of marginal relevance: they should not reduce the sentence through their effect on community protection; hardship should not be presumed from the prospect of an application; and they are an unavoidable consequence of imprisonment not given special mitigatory weight. (Commonwealth regime; outside the app’s Victorian scope.)

refs.q: The potential relevance of continuing detention orders to sentencing is marginal. Assuming that they may have some relevance, they should not have such an effect on the relevance of community protection and incapacitation as to result in a reduction in the sentence imposed.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

refs.q: Moreover, a court should not infer or presume the existence of hardship from the prospect an offender might be subject to an application for a continuing detention order that will make their imprisonment more burdensome.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

refs.q: The potential application of this part is an incident of the offending and of the sentences imposed that is to be regarded as an unavoidable consequence of imprisonment and must not be given special mitigatory weight.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

refs.q: The Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 105A.3 provides that a continuing detention order, which requires an offender to be detained after the end of their sentence, may be made in relation to any offender convicted of, generally speaking, terrorism related offences and: • who is serving a sentence of imprisonment and will be at least 18 years old when the sentence ends; or • who is under a continuing detention order or interim detention order.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

refs.q: The maximum duration of a continuing detention order is three years, although a court may make successive continuing detention orders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

refs.q: Section 105A.23 provides that, when a court sentences an offender for a terrorism related offence it must warn them that an application for a continuing detention order may be made.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.3 – Continuing detention orders

title: Public opprobrium and loss of career
statement: Loss of reputation may be punishment, but it is unclear whether opprobrium from conviction may be considered (tension with the offender’s position of privilege or power; flag.public_opprobrium_unclear → caution). Held relevant in few instances: serious or significantly damaging publicity causing hardship; loss of career from conviction (less arguable if the career was used to offend; incidental loss may mitigate where the offending was remote from the employment).

refs.q: An offender’s loss of reputation may be a form of punishment. However, it is unclear whether opprobrium as a result of conviction may be considered by the court in sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.1 – Public opprobrium

refs.q: There is a tension between the recognition of the additional loss that conviction will visit upon an offender, against the fact that, unlike many who come before the courts, the offender occupied (or possibly even exploited) a position of privilege or power during the term of their offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.1 – Public opprobrium

refs.q: if serious and/or significantly damaging publicity arising from a proceeding generated hardship to the offender;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.1 – Public opprobrium

refs.q: where an offender loses their career as the result of being convicted for criminal offending. However, any mitigation may be less arguable if the offender used their career to commit the offending. Conversely, where the offending conduct is remote from the employment, the incidental loss of career may be mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.1 – Public opprobrium

title: Injury or loss suffered by the offender in the offending (extra-curial punishment)
statement: Injury or loss suffered in or as a direct consequence of the offending is generally taken into account (self-infliction is not a complete answer), but not in every case. It takes its place in the synthesis, bearing on just punishment, weight of remorse, and deterrence. To mitigate it must add to the burden of imprisonment and constitute extra-curial punishment (the test is framed for custody; for non-custodial outcomes its application is unclear — flag.extra_curial_test_scope: caution). Mental illness counts only in strictly limited circumstances: illness caused by the offender’s reaction to the consequences of offending (e.g. fear of prison) is not additional punishment. Counter-example: in R v Taylor a claimed sexually transmitted disease contracted in committing rape was not taken into account.
note: (app policy) apply limb (a) of the Delzoppo test (adds to the burden of imprisonment) to custodial outcomes; for other outcomes, caution rather than fail.

refs.q: culpable driving causing death where offender suffered serious injury in the collision;

examples.text: counter-example: claimed STD contracted in committing rape not taken into account (R v Taylor)

refs.q: But in R v Taylor, the Court dismissed an offender’s claim that the sexually transmitted disease he claimed to have contracted in the course of committing the crime of rape should be taken into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: Where an offender suffers an injury or loss in the course of, or as a direct consequence of, their offending, this is a matter that a sentencing court will generally take into account. Courts dealing with offenders who have suffered loss and injury as the result of their crimes have found that it is not a complete answer that the offender brought the injuries upon themselves.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: But this factor does not apply in mitigation of every case involving loss or injury to the offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: Injury or loss to the offender generally ‘take its place as one of the matters to be taken into account in the development of an appropriate synthesis’. Injury or loss to the offender may assume significance in the assessment of the just punishment required, the weight to be given to expressions of remorse or to general and specific deterrence in the circumstances of the particular matter.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: For the injury or loss to be mitigating, the offender will need to argue that the loss or injury would (a) add to the burden of the appellant’s imprisonment; and (b) constitute a form of extra-curial punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: And although no distinction is to be drawn between mental illness and physical injury, the circumstances in which mental illness will count as additional punishment are strictly limited. Specifically, where the illness is caused by the offender’s reaction to the consequences of the offending (e.g., fear of imprisonment), it is not an additional punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: A distinction must be drawn, no matter how difficult that may be to do, ‘between a mental condition caused by the offending and one caused by the offender’s reaction to the offending’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

title: The plea: committal warning; encouragement; the “illogicality” with not-guilty pleas
statement: On committal for trial the magistrate must inform the accused that the sentencing court may consider any plea and its timing. The Manual (7.1.1, in the present tense) says courts must actively encourage pleas to relieve strains on the system; whether this still applies is the currency question in flag.covid_custody_currency. The Manual notes a “certain illogicality” between the plea discount and the rule that a not guilty plea is never aggravating.

refs.q: Moreover, when an accused is being committed for trial, the magistrate must inform them that the sentencing court may consider any plea and the stage at which it is given.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: Given the circumstances, courts must provide actual encouragement to relieve strains on the system by encouraging the accused to plead guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: Clearly there is a ‘certain illogicality’ between the principle of a guilty plea discount and the prohibition on treating a plea of not guilty as aggravating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

title: Plea and other mitigation under a mandatory minimum: little authority
statement: A mandatory minimum can complicate reductions for mitigating factors, including the plea: a minimum regime does not oust common law principles but modifies them, and there is little authority on mitigation in mandatory regimes. A plea cannot itself take the sentence below a statutory minimum: an early guilty plea may not be considered in deciding whether there are substantial and compelling reasons (the fourth special reason), and none of the other three special reasons concerns a plea (mm.special_reason). (app policy) How mitigation operates above the minimum is an evaluative matter: the reasoning should say how it applied it.

refs.q: A mandatory minimum term of imprisonment can create complications for reductions in sentence for mitigatory factors, including pleas of guilty. A minimum sentencing regime does not oust common law sentencing principles but necessarily modifies both.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment

refs.q: There is little authority available on the question of mitigation in the context of mandatory sentencing regimes; the issue is likely to arise more frequently as the number of offences subject to minimum sentencing requirements increases.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment

title: Section 6AAA: transparency, artificiality, and the effect of non-compliance
statement: The common law requires the justification for a sentence reduction to be transparent. Questions remain about which aspects of the plea are quantified (utilitarian value alone, or remorse and acceptance of responsibility too); in Victoria the preference is to take each aspect of the plea together (s6aaa.method). The Court of Appeal has noted the artificiality of the hypothetical post-trial sentence. Section 6AAA states no consequence for failing to specify the discount, and the Act provides that failing to give reasons or comply with another procedural requirement does not invalidate a sentence; but the Court of Appeal has used the s 6AAA statement, with other factors, to find error.

refs.q: The common law holds that the justification for a sentence reduction must be transparent.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence

refs.q: Should the utilitarian value of the plea be isolated, for example, while other aspects of the plea such as the presence of remorse or an acceptance of responsibility are left out of this analysis?
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing

refs.q: The hypothetical post-trial sentence was also the subject of comment in Samac v The Queen when the Court noted the difficulty of declaring the hypothetical sentence after trial; sentencing facts cannot sensibly be presumed to coincide with the evidence led at the hypothetical trial, which resulted in the presumed guilty verdict.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.5 – Further difficulties

title: Sentence indications: when they can be given and whom they bind
statement: A magistrate’s power to indicate is engaged only once summary jurisdiction has been invoked. An indication binds only the judicial officer who gave it, not a hearing before a different judge or magistrate; the court may impose a less severe sentence type or total effective sentence than indicated. Courts generally decline to indicate where the decision turns on material not yet before them; the express reference to victim impact does not displace the other mandatory considerations.

refs.q: However, a magistrate’s power to give a sentence indication is only engaged once summary jurisdiction has been invoked: the legislative purpose of the sentencing indication is not so broad as to encompass a sentence indication where the Magistrates’ Court had no power to deal with the charge.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.1 – Magistrates’ Court

refs.q: A sentence indication only binds the magistrate who gives the indication. It does not bind the court on any hearing before a different judge or magistrate.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.1 – Magistrates’ Court

refs.q: But the court may sentence the offender to a less severe sentence type or maximum total effective sentence than stated in the sentence indication.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.2 – Higher courts

refs.q: Sentencing courts will generally decline to give an indication where the decision turns upon material that is not yet before the court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.3 – Discretionary considerations

refs.q: The specific reference to the impact on any victim does not mean the other mandatory considerations do not need to be considered at the sentence indication stage.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.3 – Discretionary considerations

title: Cooperation: known witnesses face greater risk; protection-prisoner classes differ
statement: It has been said that an offender who undertakes to give evidence becomes a known offender facing a notorious and grave risk of reprisal, unlike one whose assistance is unknown. Protection prisoners are not treated equally: more leniency is given to a prisoner in protection because of cooperation than to others (e.g. corrupt police officers, sex offenders). The risk to informers can never be accurately measured, but where there is a real risk the court must adjust the sentence (this is not bowing to criminals), within the instinctive synthesis — not by fixing a sentence and then departing from it.

refs.q: However, it has been said that an offender who undertakes to give such evidence becomes a known offender who faces a notorious and grave risk of reprisal, in contrast to an offender whose assistance is unknown and so is not exposed to a present risk.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.7 – Consequences for cooperating offender(s)

refs.q: The different protection prisoners are not necessarily treated equally. The leniency to be given to a prisoner placed in protection because of cooperation is greater than that allowed other protection prisoners, for example corrupt police officers and sex offenders.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Such a risk can never be accurately measured. Nevertheless, in circumstances where there is a real risk that the threats will be carried out, a court must adjust the sentence accordingly. To do so does not involve ‘bow[ing] to pressure from criminals’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Assessment of the risk must factor into the instinctive synthesis. A sentencing judge must not determine an appropriate sanction in the absence of a risk and then consider whether the risk provides a sufficient basis to depart from the otherwise appropriate sanction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: Informers may be exposed to threats of future harm.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

title: Prevalence: procedural fairness has displaced the “notorious prevalence” cases
statement: Earlier cases said the prevalence of some offences was so notorious that no proof or prior canvassing was required; the better view now is that any reliance on prevalence requires procedural fairness and disclosure of the source of the reasoning.

refs.q: There are earlier cases that state the prevalence of some offences is so notorious that no proof, and no prior canvassing of the issue is required. However, the better view is now that any reliance on prevalence as a sentencing factor demands the court afford the parties procedural fairness on the issue and disclose the source of the reasoning.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

title: Delay: the incongruity of systemic delay; prospective rehabilitation
statement: It is incongruous to say an offence is so serious that stern sentences are needed while sanctioning a leisurely progression of proceedings over years. Prospective rehabilitation during delay may warrant mitigation by a merciful approach and a disposition directed at rehabilitation or an earlier return to the community.

refs.q: It is incongruous, on one hand, to assert that an offence is so serious the courts must limit its occurrence by imposing stern sentences, and, on the other hand, sanctioning a ‘leisurely progression of the criminal justice proceedings which follow its commission that literally years pass before the matter comes before the court, on the other’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.2 – Systemic responsibility

refs.q: Prospective rehabilitation may warrant mitigation of sentence by authorising a merciful approach and by indicating the imposition of a disposition directed at rehabilitation, or at least, the earlier return of the offender to the community.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.4 – Consequences of delay > 7.5.4.2 – Rehabilitation limb

title: Fresh evidence of hardship on appeal: examples; family hardship cases
statement: Fresh evidence of hardship may be admitted on appeal where it shows the true significance of facts existing at sentence — e.g. an assault on an informer after incarceration showing the risk had eventuated, or a significant medical diagnosis that increases the burden of imprisonment and the risk of a gravely adverse effect on health. The decided third-party hardship cases concern mostly hardship to the offender’s family from imprisonment.

refs.q: For example: evidence of an assault on a police informer after incarceration may be admitted on appeal and ameliorate the sentence on the basis that the risk to the offender had eventuated and imposed a heavier burden than was foreseeable at the original time of sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.3 – Fresh evidence of hardship in custody

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has accepted that the diagnosis may increase both the burden of imprisonment on an applicant and the serious risk it will have a gravely adverse effect on their health.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.3 – Fresh evidence of hardship in custody

refs.q: • evidence of consequences of a shot gun injury found to increase the burden of imprisonment;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.4 – Ill health

refs.q: The decided cases are overwhelmingly concerned with hardship to the offender’s family when the offender must serve a term of imprisonment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: Most often, fresh evidence is sought to be admitted where a significant medical condition emerges after sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.3 – Fresh evidence of hardship in custody

title: Forfeiture as punishment: proceeds vs punitive forfeiture; future forfeiture; tainted property
statement: Forfeiting proceeds of crime restores the offender’s prior position and is not punishment; an order going beyond that (or relating to previously owned property) may be punitive and considered — a “clear distinction”. Future forfeiture may be taken into account if there is enough evidence to assess its likelihood and effect; if not, there is no error in disregarding it. The offender bears the onus; for lawfully acquired “tainted” property the punitive element must be sufficiently identified.

refs.q: There is a ‘clear distinction’ between an order forfeiting the proceeds of crime and one that punishes by going beyond what is required simply to prevent the offender from profiting from their crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.1 – Forfeiture orders

refs.q: There will be no error committed if the information available is insufficient to enable the court to assess the likelihood and effect of future forfeiture.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.2 – Future forfeiture

refs.q: The offender bears the onus of establishing forfeiture as a mitigating circumstance. Where lawfully acquired property has been used in the commission of a crime and it is ‘tainted’ property the punitive element of its forfeiture must be sufficiently identified for it to be considered in mitigation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.3 – Onus of proof

refs.q: How much of the property was lawfully acquired, the offender’s interest in the property and the extent to which it was used to facilitate the commission of the crime may all require proof.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders > 7.7.1.3 – Onus of proof

title: Extra-curial punishment: not every self-inflicted loss counts
statement: In R v Taylor (Victorian Court of Criminal Appeal, 1974: fn 1729) the Court dismissed an offender’s claim that a disease contracted in committing rape should be taken into account; injury or loss generally takes its place as one matter in the synthesis.

refs.q: But in R v Taylor, the Court dismissed an offender’s claim that the sexually transmitted disease he claimed to have contracted in the course of committing the crime of rape should be taken into account.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending

refs.q: Injury or loss to the offender generally ‘take its place as one of the matters to be taken into account in the development of an appropriate synthesis’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.8 – Punishment from other sources > 7.8.2 – Injury or loss sustained in offending
